articles.title: BBC Inside Science - The Mathematical Revolution - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: One of the greatest problems in the history of mathematics has been solved by AI.
articles.body: Could AI have solved mathematics’ greatest mystery? The Riemann Hypothesis has baffled mathematicians for 165 years, but mathematician Levent Alpoge believes he has found a proof, working with AI system Claude. Tom Whipple and mathematician Kit Yates explore what this could mean for mathematics and the humans who dedicate their lives to it. Plus, head to the University of Reading to discover how an Allosaurus ate its prey. With the help of a contraption called Dinosaw and a roast chicken, Manabu Sakamoto is trying to understand how the teeth of these prehistoric predators cut through flesh. Produced in partnership with The Open University. articles.title: 'Musa do Jihad' começa a ser julgada em Paris | G1
articles.standfirst: Émilie König, de 41 anos, virou uma das vozes femininas mais influentes do Estado Islâmico, grupo terrorista que cometeu série de atentados na Europa há cerca de uma década. König vai tentar provar no tribunal anterrorista de Paris que rompeu com o grupo.
articles.summary: Émilie König, de 41 anos, virou uma das vozes femininas mais influentes do Estado Islâmico, grupo terrorista que cometeu série de atentados na Europa há cerca de uma década.
articles.body:
A francesa Émilie König, que será julgada pela Justiça da França por ter se unido ao Estado Islâmico na Síria, em imagem de 2018. — Foto: Divulgação/ serviço de imprensa do YPG

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Uma das figuras femininas mais conhecidas do extremismo islâmico na França começou nesta quinta-feira (26) a responder perante o tribunal antiterrorista de Paris por sua adesão ao grupo Estado Islâmico , o grupo terrorista jihadista que cometeu uma série de atentados na Europa há cerca de uma década.

👉 Aos 41 anos, a francesa Émilie König ficou conhecia como “musa do jihad” ao deixar a França para se unir às fileiras do Estado Islâmico na Síria. De volta a seu país após ser presa na Síria, ela agora enfrenta um julgamento que poderá resultar em até 30 anos de prisão e que deve servir também como teste para a Justiça avaliar se integrantes do grupo podem ser reabilitados .

Durante anos, seu nome circulou entre os serviços de inteligência internacionais como o de uma das vozes femininas mais influentes da propaganda do Estado Islâmico .

Nesta quinta-feira (26), porém, Émilie König apareceu diante do tribunal especial antiterrorismo de Paris não mais como símbolo do jihadismo europeu, mas como uma ré que tenta convencer a Justiça de que rompeu definitivamente com o extremismo .

A francesa responde por associação criminosa com finalidade terrorista após ter se juntado ao Estado Islâmico na Síria e participado da máquina de propaganda da organização. Ela está detida desde seu repatriamento para a França, em 2022.

O julgamento também coloca em discussão um tema que acompanha a França desde o colapso do autoproclamado califado: como lidar com cidadãos franceses que aderiram ao projeto jihadista, viveram sob o domínio do Estado Islâmico e posteriormente retornaram ao país.

Uma das primeiras francesas a viajar para a Síria

Jornalistas aguardam no tribunal antiterrorista de Paris, na França, o início do julgamento da francesa Emilie Konig, que se uniu ao grupo terrorista Estado Islâmico, em 26 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Gonzalo Fuentes/ Reuters

Nascida na Bretanha, no oeste francês, König foi uma das primeiras mulheres francesas a viajar para a Síria, ainda em 2012 . Na época, o Estado Islâmico consolidava sua presença na região e atraía simpatizantes estrangeiros de diversos países europeus .

Segundo a acusação, sua atuação foi além do simples apoio ideológico . Os promotores afirmam que ela exerceu funções de recrutadora, intermediária e propagandista , utilizando intensamente as redes sociais para divulgar mensagens favoráveis ao grupo extremista e incentivar a partida de simpatizantes para as zonas controladas pelo chamado califado.

A notoriedade adquirida dentro do universo jihadista levou Émilie König a uma situação inédita. Em 2014, ela se tornou a primeira mulher incluída na lista de sanções das Nações Unidas por envolvimento com o terrorismo . No ano seguinte, foi uma das duas primeiras mulheres a integrar também a lista de sanções dos Estados Unidos.

As autoridades norte-americanas sustentaram à época que ela havia incentivado ataques contra instituições francesas. O Ministério Público Nacional Antiterrorista francês afirma que a acusada alimentava "massivamente" suas redes sociais com conteúdos de apoio ao Estado Islâmico.

Entre os elementos apresentados no processo, estão mensagens particularmente violentas. Em uma publicação de 2014, König escreveu que a França pagaria com sangue por suas ações militares .

Em 2017, em uma mensagem enviada à própria mãe, afirmou que, caso retornasse ao território francês, pretendia cometer um atentado suicida contra os "inimigos de Alá" , evocando os ataques de novembro de 2015 em Paris, incluindo o massacre na casa de espetáculos Bataclan.

A própria investigação, entretanto, concluiu que parte da imagem construída em torno da acusada era maior do que seu papel efetivo dentro da organização terrorista.

Ao encerrar anos de apurações, os juízes de instrução reconheceram que Émilie König possuía influência junto a simpatizantes do grupo, mas observaram que ela também contribuiu para alimentar uma reputação superior à sua posição real.

Segundo os magistrados, a francesa chegou a atribuir a si mesma determinadas funções dentro da estrutura do Estado Islâmico que jamais exerceu.

Ainda assim, os investigadores concluíram que sua ideologia era particularmente radical e que sua atividade de propaganda teve impacto concreto na difusão da mensagem jihadista .

Sua trajetória pessoal também deverá ocupar espaço importante durante o julgamento. Antes de partir para a Síria, ela deixou na França os dois filhos que já tinha e se juntou a um homem ligado a uma rede jihadista da cidade de Nîmes, com quem se casou.

O companheiro morreu posteriormente em operações do próprio Estado Islâmico.

Já em território sírio, ela teve outros três filhos , nascidos entre 2015 e 2017. Segundo a acusação, a constituição dessa nova família fazia parte do projeto social e demográfico defendido pela organização extremista para consolidar o chamado califado.

Para a defesa, no entanto, o foco do julgamento não deve ser o retrato construído ao longo dos anos pela mídia e pelos serviços de segurança, mas a análise concreta dos fatos atribuídos à acusada.

Seu advogado, Emmanuel Daoud, afirma que Émilie König pretende demonstrar seu "desengajamento" em relação à ideologia extremista e provar que não apresenta mais risco à sociedade. Segundo ele, avaliações realizadas por especialistas apontam uma evolução considerada positiva desde sua captura e posterior repatriação.

A estratégia da defesa também passa por explicar as circunstâncias pessoais que contribuíram para sua radicalização. O objetivo, segundo Daoud, não é justificar os atos praticados, mas oferecer elementos que permitam compreender o percurso que a levou ao jihadismo.

A aposta é ambiciosa. Poucos nomes permaneceram tão associados à propaganda do Estado Islâmico na França quanto o de Émilie König.

O julgamento que começou nesta quinta-feira deverá decidir se a mulher que durante anos encarnou a imagem da "musa do jihad" pode convencer a Justiça de que deixou esse passado para trás.

articles.title: Rio Poti recebe esgoto sem tratamento em 18 pontos de Teresina | G1
articles.standfirst: O trecho entre a Ponte Juscelino Kubitschek e a nova ponte da UFPI concentra 6 pontos de lançamento irregular de esgoto sem tratamento direto no rio.
articles.summary: Levantamento da Arsete aponta que o Rio Poti recebe esgoto sem tratamento em 18 pontos de Teresina, problema agravado por ligações irregulares em galerias pluviais.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O Rio Poti recebe 18 pontos de lançamento de esgoto sem tratamento na área urbana de Teresina, segundo levantamento da Águas de Teresina feito a pedido da Agência Municipal de Regulação de Serviços Públicos de Teresina (Arsete).

De acordo com o relatório, o trecho entre a Ponte Juscelino Kubitschek, na Avenida Frei Serafim, e a nova ponte da Universidade Federal do Piauí (UFPI), ainda em construção, concentra uma das maiores quantidades de despejos irregulares.

Nesse trecho, foram identificados seis pontos de lançamento de esgoto sem tratamento diretamente no rio.

A Arsete esclareceu que os pontos de lançamento irregular de esgoto são diferentes dos despejos feitos pelas Estações de Tratamento de Esgoto (ETEs) da Águas de Teresina.

Segundo a agência, as estações têm autorização da Agência Nacional de Águas e Saneamento Básico (ANA) para lançar os efluentes nos rios após o tratamento. Por isso, esses despejos não são considerados irregulares.

De acordo com técnicos da Arsete, o principal problema é o esgoto que chega ao rio Poti sem passar pela rede de coleta e tratamento.

A agência também informou que muitos moradores ainda não fizeram a ligação de seus imóveis à rede de esgoto, mesmo em ruas que já contam com a infraestrutura.

Nesses casos, o esgoto é lançado nas valetas das ruas e acaba chegando às galerias pluviais, que deveriam receber exclusivamente água da chuva e direcioná-la aos rios.

A força-tarefa remove aguapés de trechos do Rio Poti

A força-tarefa que remove aguapés de trechos do Rio Poti, em Teresina , já retirou um volume de plantas aquáticas suficiente para cobrir um campo de futebol com uma camada de aproximadamente 3,5 centímetros de vegetação.

Segundo a Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente (Semam), cerca de 525 metros cúbicos de aguapés foram recolhidos desde o início da operação, na segunda-feira (23).

A ação deve durar cerca de 45 dias, reunindo órgãos ambientais estaduais e municipais, além da Águas de Teresina.

Segundo Roncalli Filho, secretário municipal de meio ambiente, o plano emergencial prevê o deslocamento dos aguapés para as margens do rio. Em seguida, as plantas serão recolhidas pelas equipes que atuam na operação.

"É um plano emergencial. A intenção é fazer o manejo dos aguapés para a margem e fazer a retirada com a retroescavadeira, colocando no caminhão e podendo dar a destinação correta", explicou o secretário.

Vista aérea de uma ponte estaiada sobre um rio com vegetação aquática densa, ladeado por árvores e com uma cidade ao fundo sob céu azul.

articles.title: Homem é preso em flagrante suspeito de estuprar enteada de 15 anos em Abaetetuba, no PA | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Polícia Civil, o suspeito buscou a adolescente na escola e desviou o caminho para uma área de mata. Ele foi encontrado em um condomínio e levado à delegacia.
articles.summary: Segundo a Polícia Civil, o suspeito buscou a adolescente na escola e desviou o caminho para uma área de mata. Ele foi encontrado em um condomínio e levado à delegacia.
articles.body:
Um policial civil, visto de costas com colete preto, acompanha um homem algemado, também de costas, em uma área externa com vegetação e um veículo escuro.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

De acordo com o relato da mãe da vítima, o homem buscou a adolescente na escola. No caminho de volta para casa, ele teria desviado o trajeto para uma área de mata, onde teria usado drogas e cometido o abuso. Depois, segundo a polícia, ele ameaçou a jovem para que ela não contasse nada à mãe. As informações foram divulgadas nesta quinta-feira (26).

A adolescente chegou chorando à casa de uma tia e contou o que tinha acontecido. A mãe, então, procurou a delegacia para registrar a ocorrência.

A polícia começou as buscas pelo suspeito. A mãe informou que ele poderia estar em casa, e a equipe foi até o endereço. Lá, os policiais encontraram a moto dele com a chave na ignição. O homem não estava no imóvel, mas foi localizado durante rondas no condomínio.

Ele foi levado à delegacia e está à disposição da Justiça. O nome do suspeito não foi divulgado.

Casos de violência sexual contra crianças e adolescentes podem ser denunciados pelo Disque 100 , de forma anônima e gratuita, ou ao Conselho Tutelar.

articles.title: Guia gastronômico 'Égua do Guia' aposta nas cozinhas de bairro para mostrar o sabor de Belém | G1
articles.standfirst: Guia com curadoria da cozinheira social Verena Aquino e fotos de Walda Marques é lançado nesta quinta-feira (26). Exemplares serão distribuídos em pontos turísticos da capital.
articles.summary: Guia com curadoria da cozinheira social Verena Aquino e fotos de Walda Marques é lançado nesta quinta-feira (26). Exemplares serão distribuídos em pontos turísticos da capital.
articles.body:
Capa do livro 'Égua do Guia' sobre gastronomia amazônica paraense. A capa mostra um prato amarelo com camarões, vegetais verdes e pimentas, ao lado de uma garrafa de bebida amarela, frutas e um pote de cerâmica em uma mesa de madeira.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Nem toda boa mesa de Belém está nos roteiros de sempre. Muitas vezes, ela está numa cozinha de bairro, comandada por quem aprendeu a receita em casa e transformou o tempero em negócio. É essa Belém que o "Égua do Guia: Gastronomia Amazônica Paraense" quer colocar no mapa. A publicação, lançada nesta quinta-feira (26), reúne 15 empreendimentos das periferias da Região Metropolitana.

O guia tem curadoria da cozinheira social Verena Aquino, fotografias de Walda Marques e texto de Pascoal Gemaque. Para chegar aos 15 nomes, a equipe percorreu os bairros em visitas técnicas, ouviu os donos dos negócios e registrou cozinhas, pratos e personagens.

Um dos endereços é o As Negonas, no Bengui, fundado por três irmãs. Para Nazaré Reis, uma das donas, entrar no guia tem gosto de conquista para o negócio e para o bairro.

Prato de comida com arroz branco, carne cozida, vegetais verdes e molho alaranjado, acompanhado por uma tigela com molho e pimentas amarelas.

"O Bengui sempre esteve fora do eixo gastronômico tradicional, então ser reconhecido como um possível destino gastronômico é uma conquista muito importante para nós. Nossa história começou com o sonho de três irmãs de empreender, e foi a nossa persistência que nos levou a lugares que nunca imaginamos", conta Nazaré.

A ideia, segundo os organizadores, é mostrar que a riqueza da culinária paraense também mora nas cozinhas de bairro e nas mãos de quem mantém vivas as tradições. Antes do lançamento, o projeto já tinha promovido, em agosto, 20 horas de oficinas no Parque da Cidade, sobre empreendedorismo, gestão, fotografia e identidade gastronômica.

Depois do lançamento, os exemplares do guia serão distribuídos em pontos turísticos da cidade, para que moradores e visitantes descubram esses endereços.

O "Égua do Guia" é uma realização do Instituto Cultural Amazônia do Amanhã (ICAA), do Impact Hub Belém e da Rede Igapó, com patrocínio do Mercado Livre e da Wilson Sons, por meio da Lei Rouanet.

articles.title: Bancos vermelhos contra feminicídio podem ser instalados em Cubatão | G1
articles.standfirst: Projeto aprovado pela Câmara segue para sanção do prefeito e prevê assentos em espaços públicos com mensagens de conscientização e telefones de atendimento às vítimas.
articles.summary: Projeto aprovado pela Câmara segue para sanção do prefeito e prevê assentos em espaços públicos com mensagens de conscientização e telefones de atendimento às vítimas.
articles.body:
Banco vermelho simboliza o combate ao feminicídio e a violência contra a mulher. - IMAGEM ILUSTRATIVA. — Foto: Ana Clara Marinho/TV Globo

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A Câmara Municipal de Cubatão (SP) aprovou, na terça-feira (24), um projeto de lei que prevê a instalação de bancos vermelhos em praças, parques, escolas e outros espaços públicos para conscientizar a população sobre a violência contra a mulher e o feminicídio . A proposta segue para sanção do prefeito.

Batizada de Banco Vermelho, a iniciativa prevê a pintura de assentos em locais de grande circulação de pessoas. Os bancos deverão conter mensagens de conscientização e os números dos canais de atendimento às vítimas:

180: Central de Atendimento à Mulher, para denúncias e orientações;

190: Polícia Militar (PM), para situações de emergência.

O projeto, de autoria do vereador Rony Martins (PSD), também autoriza a prefeitura a instalar novos bancos em espaços públicos onde não houver assentos disponíveis. A execução da iniciativa dependerá de avaliação do Poder Executivo.

Na mesma sessão, os vereadores aprovaram, em segunda discussão, um projeto de lei que prevê transporte público gratuito para gestantes, mulheres no período pós-parto e pacientes em tratamento contra o câncer em Cubatão.

De autoria do vereador Allan Matias (PSD), o Projeto de Lei nº 62/2026 tem como objetivo facilitar o acesso dessas pessoas a consultas, exames e tratamentos de saúde.

Projeto de Cubatão (SP) promete trazer visibilidade sobre a violência contra a mulher. — Foto: Giuliano Gomes/PR PRESS

articles.title: Black Friday: torrefação santista de 1912 dá até 25% off em cafés da casa | G1
articles.standfirst: A Black do Rei do Café vai de 23 a 29 de novembro, no site da casa, com Tradicional, Gourmet, especiais e kits em promoção, e a casa indica qual café levar conforme o paladar.
articles.summary: A Black do Rei do Café vai de 23 a 29 de novembro, no site da casa, com Tradicional, Gourmet, especiais e kits em promoção, e a casa indica qual café levar conforme o paladar.
articles.body:
Três embalagens de café da marca Rei do Café, nas versões Tradicional (verde), Especial (bege) e Gourmet (marrom), estão sobre uma mesa de madeira com grãos de café espalhados.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O Rei do Café, torrefação em operação desde 1912 no Centro Histórico de Santos, faz de 23 a 29 de novembro a Black do Rei, com desconto nos cafés vendidos no site da casa: Tradicional, Gourmet e kits com 20%, e especiais com até 25%. Pedidos acima de R$ 99 têm entrega sem custo para todo o estado de São Paulo, e o pedido também pode ser retirado na loja da Rua Gonçalves Dias, no Centro.

A Black Friday acontece em 27 de novembro, e a torrefação estendeu a ação para a semana inteira. Junto com o desconto, a casa passou a orientar a compra pelo paladar, para responder a uma dúvida que, segundo os proprietários, é a mais comum no balcão: qual café levar.

"Há quem aproveite para abastecer a casa com o Tradicional ou o Gourmet e há quem queira experimentar um café diferente. A Black serve para os dois, e a ficha no pacote ajuda nessa escolha", diz Guilherme Mauri, proprietário do Rei do Café, negócio familiar hoje na terceira geração.

Segundo Ariel Ukmar, mestre de torra da casa, a primeira pergunta é como a pessoa toma café hoje. Para quem prefere uma bebida mais forte e encorpada, a indicação é o Tradicional , o café que fez a fama da casa: 100% arábica, em torra escura, com aquele amargor que o brasileiro gosta. Para quem toma sem açúcar ou procura uma xícara mais suave, o Gourmet , de torra média e com grãos selecionados acima de 82 pontos, preserva a doçura natural do grão.

Os dois entram na Black com 20% de desconto. O Tradicional sai em pacotes de 250 e 500 gramas, e o Gourmet chega ao pacote de 1 quilo, em grão ou moído, o que ajuda quem quer abastecer a casa até o começo do ano.

"A escolha funciona por degrau, e cada degrau muda pouca coisa de cada vez", afirma Ukmar.

O degrau seguinte é o café especial, classificação reservada aos lotes que passam de 80 pontos numa escala até 100 , pelo protocolo da Specialty Coffee Association (SCA). No pacote, o consumidor encontra a ficha do lote: variedade, região, altitude, processo e produtor. Na Black, os especiais saem com até 25% de desconto.

Para a primeira compra, a casa indica o Catuaí Vermelho , da Fazenda Santa Lúcia, em Varginha, no Sul de Minas, de xícara limpa e equilibrada. Para doçura, o Bourbon Amarelo , de Nepomuceno. Para uma xícara equilibrada da Serra da Canastra, o Mundo Novo , da produtora Fernanda Pacheco, da Fazenda Quilombo, em Piumhi. Quem já conhece especiais encontra lotes mais raros, como o Geisha da Fazenda Santa Mônica, na Alta Mogiana, avaliado com 89 pontos.

A linha tem ainda o Especial Descafeinado , blend do Cerrado Mineiro com 81,5 pontos, em que a cafeína é retirada com água, no processo Mountain Water. Ele também entra na Black, com 10% de desconto.

Para quem prefere não escolher antes de provar, o Kit Descoberta reúne os três degraus em uma única caixa: 500 gramas do Tradicional, 500 gramas do Gourmet e 250 gramas do especial Bourbon Amarelo, num total de 1,25 quilo. Na Black, os kits da casa saem com 20% de desconto.

"Vale tomar os três na mesma semana, no mesmo método de preparo. É quando a diferença entre eles aparece", diz Ukmar.

No pedido, a moagem é escolhida conforme o preparo: coador, espresso, cafeteira italiana, prensa francesa ou árabe, turco e grego, além da opção em grão, que conserva os aromas por mais tempo. Depois de aberto, o pacote deve ficar bem fechado, longe da luz e do calor do fogão, e fora da geladeira.

Pela medida recomendada pela Associação Brasileira da Indústria de Café (Abic), de 80 a 100 gramas de pó por litro de água, um pacote de 250 gramas rende de 25 a 31 xícaras de 100 mililitros.

Para participar, basta acessar o site do Rei do Café , escolher os cafés, o tamanho do pacote e a moagem, e finalizar o pedido. Na hora de fechar a compra, o cliente escolhe entre receber em casa, com entrega sem custo para todo o estado de São Paulo em pedidos acima de R$ 99, ou retirar na loja do Centro.

articles.summary: Projeto aprovado pela Câmara prevê R$ 17 milhões para ajudar famílias de baixa renda a pagar a entrada de imóveis; proposta ainda depende de sanção e regulamentação.
articles.body:
Pessoas caminham em uma praça arborizada com palmeiras, em frente a um edifício branco com detalhes verdes e o letreiro 'COHAB', sob um céu claro.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Famílias de baixa renda de Cuiabá poderão receber uma ajuda financeira de até R$ 25 mil para pagar a entrada de um financiamento habitacional. A Câmara Municipal aprovou por unanimidade, nesta quinta-feira (26), o projeto que cria o programa Minha Entrada , que prevê R$ 17 milhões em recursos federais para essa finalidade.

A proposta, de autoria da Prefeitura, segue agora para sanção do prefeito Abilio Brunini. Para começar a atender as famílias, o programa ainda precisará ser regulamentado, com a definição dos critérios de seleção e dos valores efetivos da ajuda.

O programa prevê ajuda financeira para famílias nas três faixas urbanas do Minha Casa, Minha Vida. O limite previsto para cada uma é:

Os valores efetivos serão definidos por decreto municipal.

O dinheiro será aplicado diretamente pela instituição financeira no financiamento. Ele poderá cobrir parte ou todo o valor da entrada e, se houver saldo, será usado para diminuir o total financiado. Portanto, o valor não será depositado diretamente na conta dos beneficiários.

Os R$ 17 milhões previstos vêm de uma emenda parlamentar federal destinada pelo senador Wellington Fagundes. Segundo o projeto, o município não precisará usar dinheiro próprio para complementar o valor.

A Secretaria Municipal de Habitação e Regularização Fundiária será responsável por selecionar os beneficiários, verificar os requisitos e encaminhar as famílias à instituição financeira.

As inscrições serão gratuitas e destinadas a famílias que comprovem residência em Cuiabá. As faixas de renda e os critérios de prioridade ainda serão definidos pelo Executivo, seguindo as regras federais.

A seleção deverá ter critérios divulgados publicamente e permitirá que os interessados apresentem recurso administrativo. A concessão da ajuda também dependerá da disponibilidade dos recursos federais, da aprovação do financiamento e da assinatura do contrato.

O Minha Entrada foi anunciado pela Prefeitura em julho deste ano. Na ocasião, a proposta previa usar os R$ 17 milhões de emenda parlamentar para ajudar famílias de baixa renda que conseguem assumir as parcelas de um financiamento, mas não têm o valor necessário para pagar a entrada do imóvel.

Na apresentação inicial, a Prefeitura informou que o benefício seria integrado ao Programa Casa Cuiabana. O projeto aprovado pela Câmara regulamenta a participação de Cuiabá no Minha Casa, Minha Vida Cidades-Emendas, do governo federal.

articles.title: Marinha retoma buscas por dois pescadores desaparecidos no Pantanal | G1
articles.standfirst: Buscas haviam sido interrompidas por causa do mau tempo; um helicóptero da Marinha auxilia nas operações.
articles.summary: Buscas haviam sido interrompidas por causa do mau tempo; um helicóptero da Marinha auxilia nas operações.
articles.body:
Homem de meia-idade, com boné preto da marca MARA e jaqueta verde militar, posa em ambiente externo com folhagem verde ao fundo.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A Marinha do Brasil retomou, nesta quinta-feira (26), as buscas pelos pescadores Janair Prudêncio, conhecido como Gê, e Israel Alves de Figueiredo, chamado de Figueiredo , desaparecidos no Pantanal de Mato Grosso do Sul. As operações foram interrompidas na quarta-feira (25), em razão do mau tempo.

As buscas contam com o apoio de um helicóptero do Esquadrão de Helicópteros de Emprego Geral do Oeste , unidade da Marinha que fica em Ladário, na região de Corumbá. Até o momento, não foram encontrados vestígios dos pescadores nem da embarcação em que estavam.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, os dois foram vistos pela última vez na quarta-feira (18), em uma área de pesca no Pantanal. Desde então, familiares e conhecidos não conseguiram mais contato com eles.

De acordo com o relato da filha de Janair à polícia, os pescadores almoçaram no barraco de um homem conhecido como Ramon Traíra. O local fica a cerca de 20 minutos de barco de um hotel flutuante.

Após o almoço, Gê e Figueiredo seguiram rio abaixo, com destino ao barraco de Amaral, a aproximadamente 60 quilômetros de distância.

A previsão era que eles chegassem ao destino ainda naquele dia. No entanto, por volta das 21h, como os pescadores não haviam aparecido, conhecidos suspeitaram de que a embarcação pudesse ter apresentado algum problema ou de que algo mais grave tivesse acontecido.

Na manhã seguinte, Ramon e Amaral percorreram o trajeto que os pescadores deveriam ter feito, mas não encontraram a embarcação nem qualquer sinal dos dois homens.

Os filhos de Figueiredo também procuraram a polícia para registrar o desaparecimento do pai. Eles relataram que o pescador estava sem celular e havia combinado de entrar em contato com a família quando chegasse ao barraco de Ramon.

O combinado foi cumprido na quarta-feira (18), às 11h45, quando Figueiredo ligou para a mãe dos filhos usando o celular de Ramon.

Os familiares também informaram que havia a suspeita de que os pescadores estivessem com dois equipamentos de internet via satélite Starlink na embarcação. No entanto, os filhos de Figueiredo disseram que não sabem se os aparelhos estavam funcionando, pois o pai não havia pago pelo serviço.

A companheira de Janair também esteve na delegacia e confirmou as informações sobre o desaparecimento.

A Marinha do Brasil informou que tomou conhecimento do desaparecimento e enviou uma equipe da Capitania Fluvial do Pantanal ao local para realizar buscas.

A corporação também abriu um Inquérito Administrativo sobre Acidentes e Fatos da Navegação (IAFN) para apurar as circunstâncias do desaparecimento e verificar se houve algum fator relacionado à segurança da navegação.

A Marinha pede que qualquer informação que possa ajudar a localizar os pescadores seja comunicada pelo telefone 185, número de emergência marítima e fluvial.

articles.title: Andy Burnham caught in north-south Skynet 6 satellite deal battle
articles.summary: North East MPs want a planned defence base to be built in Sedgefield.
articles.body:
Britain is about to decide who should build a new generation of military satellites that will be vital for our armed forces in any future war.

But the contest between the two remaining rival bidders seems to have embroiled Andy Burnham's government in a home-grown north-south conflict about where the jobs and investment should go.

And MPs and local political leaders in north-east England see it as a test about just how serious the prime minister is about meeting his goal of "growth in every postcode".

Lockheed Martin wants to bring the work on the government's Skynet 6 programme to a new £85m factory in County Durham - and the site at NetPark in Sedgefield is in an area which certainly needs the 500 jobs being promised.

But supporters of rival bidder Airbus have said that will come at a huge cost in jobs at the company's sites in Portsmouth and Stevenage in the south and east of England.

And like many battles, this one has posed a challenge in sifting propaganda from truth.

At its heart is a vital decision. These satellites will be crucial to UK national security as they will carry encrypted secret communications for our armed forces.

With space now becoming increasingly militarised and a potential theatre of war, it will be vital they are as safe as possible from attack.

The government began the bidding process for the £2bn contract in May 2023, but as a decision has got closer, the contest has become more intense.

Officially the two remaining companies still in the race, Lockheed Martin and Airbus, cannot advocate publicly for their respective bids.

But there is a proxy war being fought, with competing arguments emerging from rival camps.

The North East's politicians are unsurprisingly gunning hard for Lockheed Martin and none harder than MP Alan Strickland, as the site would be in his Newton Aycliffe and Spennymoor constituency.

He has pointed to the growing number of North East firms working in the space sector as evidence the region can deliver.

A centre dedicated to the industry is also soon to open at Northumbria University in Newcastle, partly funded by £15m from Lockheed Martin.

The North East Space Skills and Technology Centre (Nesst) could provide vital research capacity and a flow of graduates for the industry.

But Strickland and other North East MPs have also pointed to a lack of defence investment in a region which has historically been one of the strongest recruiting grounds for the armed forces.

According to the latest government figures, while the Ministry of Defence (ModD) invested almost £8.5bn in industry in the South East of England last year, it only invested £200m in the North East. That was lower per head of population than any other part of the UK

Strickland said: "We've got a proud military heritage in our region but despite that we get less than 1% of all MoD spending.

"We feel as North East MPs we can do better. This satellite contract is a real opportunity to invest in the region, creating jobs and opportunities and making sure we have genuinely got growth in every postcode."

But in recent weeks the trade union Unite has been dialling up its own rhetoric on behalf of its members working at Airbus's factories in Portsmouth and Stevenage.

Airbus has won previous UK military satellite contracts and the union has said losing out could cost up to 3,000 jobs at those sites. There is concern in Wales too about the impact on work carried out at sites in Newport and Broughton.

It has also cast doubt on Lockheed Martin's plans for Sedgefield, implying that much of the work might take place in the US, where the company has its headquarters.

The union's general secretary Sharon Graham has said the government could end up "shooting itself in the foot" if it makes the wrong decision.

Unite's head of manufacturing Peter Hughes said: "Is it a promise that's actually going to be delivered?

"At the moment, they haven't even put a spade in the ground to build this factory.

"Are they actually going to be well-paid jobs, or are they just going to be assembly jobs, not specialised posts in research and development?

"It's important jobs are in the North East but not if it means getting one job in the North East means losing five jobs elsewhere. That doesn't make sense."

Unite has also questioned the wisdom of handing such a sensitive contract to a company whose ultimate headquarters is in the US.

It has raised the spectre of recent events in Ukraine where the country's armed forces have been hindered in their battle against Russia by l imits on their access to parts of the Starlink satellite system developed by Elon Musk.

This is scaremongering, according to supporters of Lockheed Martin who have said the contract would leave complete control over the satellites with the UK government, with no possibility of US interference.

They have also cast doubt on the potential jobs impact.

Lockeed's backers have also said preparatory work on access has already begun at the Sedgefield site and it could be up and running within two years, rather than the five years Unite have suggested it could take to build the factory.

The company has also already supplied the UK with vital and sensitive defence equipment that includes the RAF's F-35 fighter jets.

A Lockheed Martin spokesman said it could not comment on the procurement process.

"Lockheed Martin UK, a British company, will establish facilities to develop an ecosystem alongside our regional partners in the North East of England to provide the UK with a sovereign space capability," they said.

"It will create jobs, supply chain opportunities, and the potential for exports. It will have a UK Design Authority and a UK Chief Engineer."

An Airbus spokesman said: ""Airbus remains fully committed to the Skynet competition and we continue to comply with all requirements and timelines set by the Ministry of Defence."

Unite's lobbying might be having an effect. A decision on the contract has been delayed.

All a MoD spokesperson would say for now is: "This is an ongoing procurement process, and no final decisions have been made."

But it is a decision with political consequences. Airbus's sites in Portsmouth and Stevenage are in constituencies Labour took in 2024 that will be targeted by the Conservatives at the next election.

And Labour's political challengers in County Durham are watching carefully too.

Reform UK took control of the county council in 2024 and its deputy leader Darren Grimes said this is a test for the prime minister.

"Andy Burnham promised a Makerfield test from within 10 Downing Street - the places that Westminster have neglected would finally get some semblance of fairness.

"I think this is the golden opportunity.

"I do think the people of County Durham would wonder why he was going back on promises he made, and it would allow the North East once more to feel it is the forgotten part of the country."

A decision might come before the end of the year, but in this battle over military hardware, Andy Burnham could face a no-win scenario in choosing between north and south.

articles.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
articles.summary: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated.
articles.body:
More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.

That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.

On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.

However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

She is far from alone, with one million homeowners facing a similar increase often because they are coming off deals that were agreed before interest rates began rising in 2022.

The Bank's report said that households facing higher payments "may need to reduce discretionary spending or draw down savings as higher energy and other essential costs feed through".

Most had savings buffers but lower-income households, including renters, had less wriggle room owing to spending a greater proportion of their income on essentials.

Early in November, the Bank raised the benchmark interest rate , which influences borrowing costs for individuals and businesses, for the first time in more than three years, from 3.75% to 4%.

The numbers could change were mortgage rates to fall, primarily if international economic volatility eased.

Even so, the Bank said around 350,000 were already projected to see monthly mortgage repayments fall when they fixed their next deal within three years.

The report also suggested there were no signs of an increase in borrowers defaulting on their loans, while UK households remained resilient.

"We have not seen the scale of mortgage arrears that we saw if you go back to earlier periods, the early 90s, the early 80s, actually even the financial crisis. And we are not seeing the scale of house repossessions, and that has to be a good thing," said the Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey.

However, separately, the Bank warned that cyber attacks had become a more prominent threat to the UK's financial stability.

Financial firms needed to "keep pace with the growing scale and sophistication of cyber threats", the report said.

articles.title: A company spent years trying to turn an old Australian coal power station into a biomass plant capable of powering 200,000 homes; a court has now upheld the rejection over environmental concerns
articles.summary: A New South Wales court has upheld the rejection of Verdant Earth Technologies' proposal to convert the Redbank Power Station into a biomass plant, citing environmental impacts over potential benefits. Conservation groups have praised the decision, raising concerns over the use of native vegetation as fuel.
articles.body: A long-running proposal to convert an ageing coal-fired power station in Australia's Hunter Valley into a biomass facility capable of supplying electricity to 200,000 homes has suffered another setback after a court upheld the rejection of the project over environmental concerns.The New South Wales Land and Environment Court dismissed an appeal by Verdant Earth Technologies against the refusal to restart the former Redbank Power Station near Singleton, according to Bioenergy Insight. The ruling upholds a decision made last year by the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC), which found that the project's environmental consequences outweighed its potential benefits.Verdant Earth has owned the site since 2018 and had been pursuing plans to establish a bioenergy hub at the former coal plant. The proposed 151-megawatt facility was expected to burn approximately 700,000 tonnes of dry material annually, using invasive native vegetation cleared from farmland in western New South Wales alongside purpose-grown energy crops.The company had estimated that the development would require more than A$70 million in capital investment. Its submission to state planners also projected 330 jobs during construction and 60 permanent positions once the facility became operational.Although the IPC acknowledged the project's potential contribution to electricity security, grid reliability and employment, it ultimately refused approval because of its environmental impact.Why the biomass project faced environmental oppositionThe court's decision has been welcomed by conservation groups, which had opposed the proposed use of native vegetation as a fuel source.Jacqui Mumford, chief executive of the Nature Conservation Council of NSW (NCC), said she hoped the ruling would end efforts to restart the Redbank facility."It was a bad project from the start," Mumford said.She argued that using native vegetation to generate electricity could encourage landholders to clear bushland to meet the plant's fuel requirements, increasing pressure on threatened wildlife and vulnerable ecosystems.The NCC chief executive also challenged the classification of invasive native species (INS), arguing that it was not based on scientific grounds. She said the organisation planned to push for changes to the state's INS legislation ahead of the March state election."It's a completely political and unscientific classification; no other state or territory in Australia has the INS classification," Mumford said.The proposed fuel supply was a central part of the disagreement. Verdant Earth had planned to use vegetation removed under government-approved land-clearing programmes, alongside purpose-grown crops. Conservation groups argued that this approach could create an incentive to clear additional native bushland.Company considers alternatives after court setbackVerdant Earth chief executive Richard Poole said he was surprised by the court's decision and had not yet reviewed the full judgment."I'm a full believer in biomass as an absolute solution for Australia's energy problems," Poole told ABC News.He said the company had reached agreements over the previous 12 months to reduce its dependence on invasive native species and accelerate plans to lower the project's emissions.Poole argued that the revised proposal should have been considered for approval, particularly because the vegetation clearing involved was part of a government-approved programme. He also pointed to the value of the existing power station equipment, which he estimated at approximately A$800 million.The court ruling has also created uncertainty around a separate proposal involving the former power station site. Verdant Earth had entered discussions with Voltic DC, a data centre developer managed by APDC, over a possible facility on neighbouring land.The arrangement was expected to explore shared infrastructure and potential electricity supply from a restarted Redbank station. Voltic DC had indicated that the partnership could allow both companies to maximise the use of the adjoining land and existing infrastructure.Poole said the court's decision had put those plans in doubt, as the proposed data centre could have benefited from electricity generated at Redbank.The company is now considering its options, with Poole saying he would consult its legal team before deciding on the next steps. He also raised the possibility of using the site for a data centre or battery storage facility instead.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Inside Liberland, the crypto ‘country’ few have heard of
articles.summary: Al Jazeera’s Antoine Allen reports on a group of people trying to build a tax-free nation.
articles.body:
I had been followed by the police before but never imagined I would be tracked by a Croatian police boat along the European Union’s longest river, the Danube, on my way to a so-called crypto bro tax-free paradise.

They did not approach us. They did not shout. They used cameras to film us while we filmed them.

Croatia says it is protecting its border from people trying to claim this disputed territory as their own country: Liberland.

The boat chase was just one of many surprises my investigation into Liberland led me to.

I secured access to Vit Jedlicka, a Czech politician and YouTuber who says he spent years trying to change his own country. He decided it could not be done, so instead he searched for a country of his own. How?

“We were looking for no-man’s land and we just googled for it,” he told me.

He found a 7sq km (2.7sq mile) forested peninsula on the west bank of the Danube, left unsettled by a border dispute between Croatia and Serbia. In 2015 he declared it the Free Republic of Liberland. Its number one rule is no taxation.

Vit is not shy about his backers. “We have lots of billionaires that signed up for citizenship,” he said. The concept of Liberland has even had long-standing support from Javier Milei, now Argentina’s president.

But Vit has been chasing this dream since 2015. What made my experience different was the people I met at Liberpulco.

Because entering Liberland risks arrest, its supporters gather at a festival up the river in Serbia. It merges the Liberland gathering with Anarchapulco, the anarcho-capitalist conference founded by Jeff Berwick.

The aspiring citizens know exactly how their views are seen from the outside. Jeff said what I was thinking.

“Most people haven’t heard about Liberland, but if they have heard of it, they usually think it’s crazy conspiracy theorists, crazy anarchists.”

He wasn’t apologising. “Anarchy is a Greek word, without rulers. We just believe that the best way for humans to coexist is without being slaves to a ruler.”

On taxes, Vit set the tone. “Taxes are just fines for being productive.”

On the state, he went further. “The state would put you in jail if you start a Ponzi scheme. But if they run a pension system, which is a Ponzi scheme, they don’t save any money.”

The conference had a series of speakers. One said: “I didn’t like the vaccines, I didn’t like the mandates. So I spoke out against that. I got into trouble.”

Another told the crowd we are living in a matrix. “Words are a spell,” he said. “That’s why we call it spelling.”

Each speaker offered advice on how to gain freedom. The fear of an overbearing government seemed to be the main thing uniting the attendees.

Vit and Jeff gave me free rein. Over the week I joined a meditation class and watched a knife defence class led by an instructor who taught himself from YouTube.

But the session on how to stop your government watching you was the one we were told not to film.

Headlines brand Liberland a playground for billionaires. So I went on a journey to track them down at the conference.

“No, no. I have a small farm, I have a few horses.”

But I discovered that the movement to set up free and self-governing communities is growing around the world. Liberland sits at one end of a spectrum that runs from homesteading to private cities such as Prospera in Honduras.

Tim Allen of the Free Cities Foundation was clear about Liberland’s biggest problem. “Your territory is only as good as you can defend it.”

Croatia rejects Liberland outright. In a statement to Al Jazeera, its Foreign Ministry called it a provocative action with no basis in law. In 2023, Croatian authorities demolished the settlement Liberlanders had built on the land.

On my last evening, I boarded Vit’s yacht in the middle of the Danube as he handed out medals and passports, with a Croatian police boat a few hundred metres away.

Two thoughts kept running through my head. The first: Am I in a James Bond film?

The second: If I am, who is the villain?

Is Liberland a scam, selling passports for a country nobody can enter without fear of arrest? Or is it simply wealthy people trying to hold on to their money, without a care for how taxes often help those in need?

The banquet auction gave me part of an answer. It wasn’t exactly a billion-dollar bidding war.

Whether they had lots of money or lived off the land, they were united by one belief: They don’t like big government, or even mainstream media.

But I kept thinking about who Liberland would leave out. When I asked Vit who could become a citizen, he was direct. “We also don’t accept people that are insolvent.”

A country with limited government also has limited safety mechanisms for people of more modest means when they fall into trouble.

Vit hopes Liberland will become a state within 15 to 20 years. “We are not teenagers yet,” he told me.

The land is real. But Liberland is still a far-off dream, with a passport you can’t use.

So I’m left with one question: Does the world need another country, especially one with freedoms only for the rich?

articles.title: How an oil feud is deepening rift between Baghdad and Iraq’s Kurdish region
articles.summary: Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s move to take control of border crossings and oilfields has drawn a sharp response from Erbil.
articles.body:
Iraq’s federal government and the semi-autonomous Kurdish region are locked in their sharpest confrontation in years over who controls the country’s oil , its border crossings and the revenues that flow from them.

The crisis escalated this week. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal authorities to take over all border crossings in the northern Kurdish region, close unofficial crossings used for smuggling, and seize control of oilfields in disputed provinces held by Kurdish security forces. Within 24 hours, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court had issued a ruling backing Baghdad’s powers.

The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has called the measures a violation of the constitution and accused Baghdad of trying to return Iraq to centralisation. On Wednesday, as reports spread that army units were heading north, the government in Baghdad insisted it had no plans to send troops into the region.

Here is what we know about the dispute, and where it could be headed.

On the surface, the dispute is about oil smuggling.

On Tuesday, al-Zaidi ordered the Border Ports Authority to take over all crossings into the Kurdish region and directed the closure of all unofficial crossings. He told the energy police to secure all oilfields. He also ordered the federal Oil Ministry to take over the management of fields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala provinces.

Those provinces lie in a belt of territory that both Baghdad and Erbil claim. The 2005 constitution set out a process under Article 140 to settle their status, but it was never completed.

Kirkuk, home to some of Iraq’s largest oilfields, has been the most bitterly contested. Kurdish forces took control of the city in 2014 after the Iraqi army withdrew from conflict with ISIL (ISIS). Federal forces retook it in October 2017, after the Kurdish region held an independence referendum which Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court later declared unconstitutional and void.

Al Jazeera correspondent Suhaib al-Asa has reported that the oil sites named in this week’s order are, in practice, outside the semi-autonomous Kurdish region but still under the control of its security forces.

The court ruling raised the stakes further. In an interpretive decision, the Federal Supreme Court affirmed the federal government’s authority to secure Iraq’s international borders and deploy the armed forces across all Iraqi territory. The court said federal authorities could supervise border crossings, including those in the Kurdish region. It also confirmed Baghdad’s power to oversee the production and export of oil and gas, as well as oil and non-oil revenues.

Both sides have framed the dispute as a constitutional battle, said Tallha Abdulrazaq, an independent international security and defence consultant based in the United Kingdom. Baghdad cites federal authority over national wealth and borders under Articles 110 and 112, while Erbil invokes shared customs administration and regional autonomy under Article 114.

“Paradoxically, both sides are right,” Abdulrazaq told Al Jazeera. “Since its adoption in 2005, Iraq’s constitution has contained contradictory and ambiguous provisions on oil and border management, making it a recurring recipe for political chaos.”

Baghdad presents its measures as a campaign against corruption and smuggling , not a move against the Kurds.

“National sovereignty is indivisible,” said al-Zaidi, who is also commander-in-chief of the armed forces. He described protecting Iraq’s wealth as “a battle for existence” in which the state would put an end to all forms of smuggling.

The orders follow an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company. Al-Zaidi also dismissed eight security and administrative officials, including the head of the Border Ports Authority, Kirkuk’s operations commander and the province’s police chief.

Government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi told state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday that there was “no truth” to reports of troops moving towards the region. He said al-Zaidi was committed to “protecting the people of the region, not threatening them”. He added that the salaries of the Kurdish region’s public employees would be secured in the 2027 budget.

Baghdad is framing the measures as part of a wider drive to secure state security. Earlier this month, Iraqi forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad, a longtime stronghold of the Iran-aligned armed group Kataib Hezbollah. According to Reuters, the group allowed the forces in under a settlement brokered by politicians.

Abdulrazaq said al-Zaidi was justified “on the narrow facts”. “Oil smuggling across unofficial crossings is real and well-documented. However, smuggling is the pretext,” he said.

The security and defence consultant described the escalation as “largely a calculated domestic manoeuvre”. In Jurf al-Sakhar, al-Zaidi faces steep hurdles, he said. Rebuilding the town, returning Sunni Arab residents displaced for 12 years and fully expelling Kataib Hezbollah all risk triggering an intra-Shia clash.

“A controlled dispute with the Kurdistan Regional Government carries far lower political costs for Baghdad than an armed confrontation among Shia factions,” he said.

Al-Zaidi also needs to show his Shia coalition partners and armed factions that “he is decisive with everyone, not just selectively targeting some Shia militias”, Abdulrazaq added. He suggested a hard line towards the Kurds “may even have been an explicit demand from those factions” at the height of the Jurf al-Sakhar standoff.

Oil is the backbone of Iraq’s economy. It accounts for the overwhelming majority of state revenue and pays the salaries of millions of public employees, including those in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

Baghdad claims smuggling is draining that wealth on a large scale. Al-Aboudi said tens of billions had gone into “private pockets and accounts” without benefiting the region’s residents. According to Al Jazeera’s al-Asa, the government estimates that 200,000 to 230,000 barrels of oil per day (bpd) are smuggled, worth about $200m a month.

Al-Asa has reported that oil is moved from the disputed provinces to other parts of Iraq and then abroad, or sent directly from Sulaimaniyah, Kirkuk and Erbil towards Iran. Most of the region’s unofficial crossings are on the Iranian border, he said.

The Iraqi News Agency has published excerpts from a government intelligence report which traces smuggling routes from Kirkuk and Sulaimaniyah to Iran and on to Afghanistan. The report also describes operations to disguise Iranian oil products so they can be passed off as Iraqi.

For Erbil, control of oil has been central to its autonomous status. In February 2022, the Federal Supreme Court ruled the region’s oil and gas law unconstitutional. The Kurdish region, which has enjoyed broad autonomy from Baghdad since the 1990s, has in the past ignored rulings by the federal court, and did so with that one.

The region’s independent exports suffered a major blow in March 2023 when the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline was halted after the International Chamber of Commerce in Paris ordered Turkiye to pay Iraq $1.5bn in damages over unauthorised crude oil exports from Iraq’s Kurdish region transported without Baghdad’s approval. Exports resumed in September 2025 under an interim deal between Iraq’s federal government, the KRG and foreign oil producers .

Revenue from border crossings matters, too. Salim Zakhour, a researcher in constitutional law and political systems who is based in Qatar, told Al Jazeera: “One of the key points of debate in the court’s decision is that it gave federal authorities oversight of revenues from non-oil fees and taxes, and I think this is one of the issues that could be contested in the court’s rulings.”

What has the Kurdistan Regional Government said?

The KRG has rejected Baghdad’s measures, calling them “a violation of the constitution and an infringement on the region’s rights”, and said it rejected “the language of threats” and a military approach to the dispute.

After a meeting on Wednesday, chaired by Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, the KRG’s Council of Ministers said it rejected “any attempt to return Iraq to a centralised system”. Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said addressing the region in “military language” did “not solve any problem”.

Erbil has said it supports efforts to fight corruption and smuggling. It has called for the dispute to be settled through dialogue and full implementation of the constitution.

Opposition to Baghdad’s measures has spilled onto the streets. On Thursday, thousands of demonstrators gathered in Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, protesting against the federal government’s move to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities. Erbil-based broadcaster Kurdistan24 reported that tens of thousands of people joined and that protesters were calling for Kurdish political unity.

The Kurdish news agency Rudaw reported that the region’s two main political parties, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), issued a joint statement that Baghdad’s decisions were “unexpected and deeply surprising”, warning that undermining the power of the Kurdish political entity is a “red line”.

But Abdulrazaq called the show of solidarity “a defensive reflex” driven by each party’s interests. A threat from Baghdad to one party is a threat to both, he said, and both risk losing the lucrative positions and budgets they have gained since the 2003 US-led invasion.

“It is therefore a pragmatic unity that will rapidly dissolve once the immediate threat recedes,” he said.

For now, Baghdad appears eager to avoid any sort of military showdown. Abdulrazaq noted that the government has denied deploying troops to the region. It has also sent Popular Mobilisation Forces chief Faleh al-Fayyad to press Kurdish authorities for cooperation.

The legal ground has shifted in Baghdad’s favour. “The court’s decision is final and decisive,” the legal researcher Zakhour said. “But the issue is not only constitutional and legal. There is a political problem.” He said Erbil had been counting on challenging the measures in court, but al-Zaidi had “pre-empted this step”.

Outside support for Erbil also looks thin. Abdulrazaq said Washington is “heavily focused on supporting Zaidi”, particularly his agenda to consolidate state authority and rein in Iran-backed Shia armed groups.

“The Kurds should not expect American backing in this dispute; if anything, Erbil is more likely to face quiet US pressure to accommodate Baghdad’s demands,” he said.

Tehran, he said, is also clearly satisfied with the pressure on Erbil. Iran is angered by the presence of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in the region and has carried out drone strikes on their camps. Abdulrazaq stressed, however, that there is “no hard evidence” that Baghdad’s timing is part of a direct quid-pro-quo with Iran over Jurf al-Sakhar.

Ankara’s calculus is more pragmatic, he said, anchored in trade, energy and border security. Turkiye has little interest in an armed crisis on its southern border that could send more refugees across, and is likely to avoid overt intervention, he said. Instead, it will quietly favour an arrangement that keeps commerce stable and curbs smuggling.

In an effort to defuse the crisis, Iraq’s four presidencies have agreed to a proposal by Supreme Judicial Council head Faiq Zaidan to hold a national dialogue on December 1. The four presidencies are those of the republic, the government, parliament and the judiciary.

Abdulrazaq said the dialogue offered “a face-saving opportunity rather than a permanent fix”. He said it could lead to a temporary compromise, such as a joint oversight mechanism that polices official crossings while closing down unofficial ones.

“Long-term, however, the underlying tensions will remain in play,” he said. “The constitution is contradictory and Iraq doesn’t have a federal law that clearly delineates who is responsible for what in the oil and gas sector. These issues will simply resurface at a later date, even if both parties want to kick the can down the road.”

articles.title: Rebecca Taylor: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
articles.summary: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.
articles.body:
A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.

Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.

The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.

She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.

Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.

The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.

The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.

"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.

All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.

However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.

The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

articles.title: Andalusia offers a glimpse into Spain’s future as far right gains ground
articles.summary: Ahead of Sunday’s election, Vox’s influence is already clear in Andalusia, where right-wing alliances reshape politics.
articles.body:
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.

All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.

As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party : “It can’t get worse than this”.

The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.

A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.

Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.

That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.

Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.

The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.

Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.

Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship , this area remained poor and largely agricultural.

As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.

In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.

‘The PP opened the door to the far-right’

But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.

A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.

“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”

The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.

Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.

Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.

Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.

Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.

Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.

Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.

Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.

Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.

But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.

“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.

Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.

The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.

Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.

Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.

At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.

“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.

In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.

Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.

In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.

In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.

In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.

Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.

The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.

Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.

In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.

“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.

Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.

Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.

Andalusia heavily relies on foreign workers for its greenhouses.

According to Govantes, the issue is not with migrants working in Spain but with them being recognised for their rights. The PSOE’s regularisation, he said, forced owners to make legal contracts, pay social security and provide benefits.

“Migrants’ work has always been tolerated as long as it was invisible and illegal. As they became visible and legal, they were accused of robbing Spanish people of jobs,” he said.
