articles.title: How the Huntingdon train attack unfolded - carriage by carriage
articles.summary: In five terrifying minutes, Anthony Williams stabbed passengers on a train between Peterborough and London. This is how it happened.
articles.body:
Footballer Jonathan Gjoshe, 22, was on the 18:25 train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on 1 November last year.

Just weeks into his first season at Scunthorpe United, Gjoshe was travelling to his home in London alongside 150 other passengers.

He was sitting at a table seat in Coach J when a figure appeared over his shoulder. The figure, dressed in black, was Anthony Williams, who had boarded the train moments earlier at Peterborough at 19:26.

CCTV captured the horror of what happened next.

The London-bound train was on time, travelling through Cambridgeshire at about 122mph (196km/h), when Williams began to walk through the carriages, stabbing people with a kitchen knife.

Gjoshe was the first person to be attacked. In the ensuing terror, passengers darted for cover, hiding in locked toilets, bike racks or under seats. Others tried to flee.

When they could run no further, some tried to defend themselves as well as other passengers by using frying pans and even throwing toasters.

Williams, who has schizophrenia, has now been found guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder.

Using court testimony and first-hand accounts from the victims, this is the story of what happened during five terrifying minutes on the train.

At 19:37, Williams walked into Coach J, where Gjoshe was sitting.

The footballer was leaning slightly into the aisle when Williams appeared over his shoulder. The pair briefly made eye contact before Williams, clutching a large kitchen knife, stabbed Gjoshe seven times, including to the shoulder and bicep.

Gjoshe's adrenaline kicked in and he jumped over the table before shouting: "I've been stabbed – run!" He later told police some passengers thought he was joking and remained seated.

Sitting across from him was Dinaria Soares, who, seeing the attack, jumped to her feet and ran towards the front of the train, away from Williams.

Two rows away was 29-year-old Sachin Balakrishnan, who had been on his way to see friends. He had his headphones on and was speaking to his partner. Hearing the screaming, he stood up to see what was happening.

Williams stabbed him in the forearm and the chest. The knife passed just centimetres away from his heart, puncturing a lung. In a desperate attempt to flee he said he then "runs and runs".

David Presland, 73, was also in Coach J. In the chaos, he fell to his hands and knees in the middle of the aisle.

Williams, now standing over him, stabbed him multiple times. Presland said he was left thinking he was going to die.

Williams ignored other passengers, including a woman and child, as he moved through the carriage.

Scott Bletcher, 50, who was sitting in a far corner seat of Coach J, was on his way home to Letchworth Garden City. He had been Christmas shopping in Newark and said he had been looking forward to eating the tapas he had bought.

He presumed there had been some sort of fight or disagreement when he saw people running down the aisle. Then Williams moved in front of him. Neither of them said a word before Williams stabbed him six times to his arm and body and moved on.

Bletcher called 999, but while he was on the phone to police he told them: "Oh my God, he's coming back." Bleeding, he managed to hide in a bike rack.

William's attack in Coach J lasted just 40 seconds. In that time, at least 15 wounds had been inflicted.

Scott Green was sitting a few seats into Coach H with his cockapoo, Poppy, who had been restless as fireworks exploded outside. It was four days before Bonfire Night.

Like Bletcher, the 52-year-old initially thought a fight had broken out. Then he felt a sudden jab to his side as Williams stabbed him.

Green tried to grab the blade but was unable to take it from Williams, who he said appeared dead in the eyes.

Poppy, his dog, went into attack mode, barking at Williams who continued down the train.

Green then picked up his bag and was thrown into a toilet by a woman. Amid the chaos, came a moment of levity.

"I don't usually get in with men I've just met," she told him.

When the attack began, Kevin Deely, 58, had his earphones in and was watching a video on his phone. He tried to help an injured David Presland and later remembered telling Williams: "You don't have to do this."

Deely threw a piece of luggage as Williams continued his attack, before he too was stabbed while trying to protect another passenger, Maisie Harrison.

The first alarm on the train was pulled at 19:38. At first, the driver, Andrew Johnson, had assumed someone was messing around.

But suddenly there was banging on his cab door and a voice on the intercom shouted: "There's a knifeman stabbing people."

Johnson had just 10 seconds to decide what to do next, quickly switching the train to the slow line towards Huntingdon.

Many of the passengers on board were returning from a football match between Nottingham Forest and Manchester United. One of them was Forest fan Stephen Crean, 61, who was sitting near the buffet car. He had just bought himself a £6 meal deal.

The carriage quickly filled around him as people were running for their lives through the train carriages, including some of those who were already injured.

Crean suddenly found himself at the door, with nothing between him and the vestibule between Coach H and G.

Faced with Williams, he began to grapple with the knifeman.

He said Williams seemed to be "on a mission". As they wrestled, Williams asked him: "Do you want to die?"

During the tussle, Crean's phone fell to the floor. Williams told him to pick it up.

Williams then continued into Coach G, where passenger James Tomlinson heard him say: "You're all going to die today."

Williams then turned around and headed towards the front of the train, passing through Coach L where CCTV showed him swigging from a bottle of fortified tonic wine.

Now hiding inside a toilet, Crean also called 999. "I'm scared," he told the operator.

With nowhere else to go, passengers in first-class Coach M were preparing to defend themselves. Staff member Samir Zitouni, 48, had managed to collect frying pans from the kitchen area to use as weapons. He also placed a walking frame in the aisle in an attempt to slow Williams down.

As Williams entered the carriage, Christina Jones, who also boarded the train at Peterborough, said she would throw her hot drink at him. "He's coming this way," someone else shouted.

Car delivery driver Raza Aslam, 44, who was travelling for work, said he had thought about taking shelter in a toilet when the attack began but decided he would not be able to live with himself if he did - especially as others were injured.

For protection, he stuffed a plastic bag with an empty coffee cup down the front of his jacket and told himself: "Better than nothing."

He was handed a frying pan by Zitouni to defend himself with - but he was quickly stabbed by Williams. He said he was in disbelief at how fast the attack had happened.

By now, the first-class carriage was full of people trying to flee from Williams.

Michael Paffett, 34, one of the few passengers in the first-class section prior to the attack, suffered a fracture to his cheekbone when Williams slashed his face.

As the chaos continued, Zitouni told Williams: "We love you, we can help you." He said he thought that was a better strategy than swearing at him.

He then tried to knock the knife out of Williams's hand.

Williams launched a "prolonged, persistent and brutal" attack, stabbing him multiple times. Medics who later treated Zitouni worried for his life.

Behind Zitouni was passenger Michael Gawthorpe, who told Williams: "Please stop - we've got kids." He remembered how Williams had said: "They're trying to kill me."

Gawthorpe had been handed a toaster from the kitchen, which he threw at Williams. He said the knifeman looked back at him and he later remembered thinking: "That was me done - I've made a mistake here." He said his mind turned to his wife and daughter.

After 15 seconds, the doors opened and passengers flooded out on to the platform at Huntingdon train station.

Zitouni walked down the platform with his white shirt stained red and collapsed, falling through the gap between the train and the platform.

Williams, now standing in a doorway, threw a bottle of tonic wine he had been swigging from.

Leaving the train, he jumped over a fence into the railway station car park.

Armed police arrived within minutes and Williams was shot with a baton gun, tasered and handcuffed.

His violent attack was brought to an end at 19:50.

Police had initially been told that nine people would likely die as a result of the attack. Yet all the victims survived.

Each had their evidence heard in court as Williams was convicted. His trial heard how Williams had "brought terror" to the train.

However, many of those onboard had tried to fend him off, putting themselves in harm's way to protect strangers.

They had, the court was told, shown extraordinary bravery.

articles.title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
articles.summary: The pair were technicians for German company Rheinmetall, according to Italy's foreign ministry.
articles.body:
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.

The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.

Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".

Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.

It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.

Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.

The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.

Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.

Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.

Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region.

The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.

Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.

"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.

"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

images.caption: A Rheinmetall facility in Kuwait was targeted by Iran, Italian and Kuwaiti authorities said

articles.title: Egypt detains driver suspected of causing Cairo fuel tanker crash and inferno that left 31 dead
articles.summary: The driver accused of sparking Cairo's deadly fuel tanker fire on the Ring Road is in custody as prosecutors detail the crash that led to the blaze.
articles.body: Egyptian authorities said Thursday that a driver suspected of causing a fuel tanker crash in Cairo — sparking a massive inferno described by a witness as "God’s hellfire" and leaving 31 dead — has been taken into custody. The deadly blaze erupted Wednesday during rush hour on a major highway surrounding the Egyptian capital, burning 27 vehicles and also leaving 26 injured. As of Thursday, traffic on the Ring Road returned to normal after most of the wreckage was cleared. "It was God’s hellfire on the Ring Road," Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver who witnessed the inferno, told The Associated Press. "People are still in shock." Another witness said to Reuters that victims were found trapped in their vehicles as "they did not have time to get out." STATE DEPARTMENT PRESSES EGYPT TO RESPECT RELIGIOUS FREEDOM AS CHRISTIAN CONVERT FACES POSSIBLE EXECUTION Video footage taken near the scene showed a blaze completely engulfing the highway as people gathered to look at the flames. Egyptian prosecutors said in a statement that authorities had detained the driver of a vehicle suspected of causing the fuel tanker to overturn, which resulted in the fire. They said the driver told investigators he was speeding between lanes when he hit the oil tanker in the rear right. He then lost control of his car and veered far to the right while one of the fuel truck’s tires burst. That caused the fuel tanker to hit the concrete wall of the highway and overturn, leading to the spill of fuel and the fire, according to the prosecutors' statement. The stretch of the highway where the fuel tanker overturned is in Waraq, a densely populated neighborhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area. PROTESTERS CALL FOR REGIME CHANGE IN IRAN FOLLOWING DEADLY CRASH THAT KILLED 13 OIL AND GAS WORKERS On Thursday, commuters and pedestrians stopped to examine the scene. Black scorch marks covered the metal railings of one of the highway exits, where pedestrians and hundreds of vehicles had been trapped Wednesday night. A high-voltage electricity line also lay twisted on the ground amid the black soot, while piles of ash lined parts of the Ring Road, according to the AP. For hours after the fire, the injured were still arriving at nearby hospitals as families gathered outside them in a mix of shock and grief. Authorities said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to the scene. Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record, the AP reported. articles.title: Fylde Council unanimously rejects tourist tax
articles.summary: Councillors said a visitor levy could reduce tourist numbers and harm local businesses.
articles.body:
A council has unanimously voted against introducing a tourist tax, warning it could deter visitors and damage the local hospitality industry.

Fylde Council rejected the proposal at a meeting on Tuesday, arguing a levy on overnight stays would have a detrimental impact on tourism and local businesses.

Under the government's Visitor Levy Bill mayors and council leaders would be able to introduce a small fee on overnight stays in their local areas - something that has previously been enforced in Edinburgh .

But councillor Michael Withers said: "This government can't help itself. Its response to everything is to tax, tax and tax again."

The Conservative and Unionist councillor continued: "I proposed that Fylde declares itself a tourist-tax free zone. I believe this will be popular with residents and with visitors. We rely on tourists – this is a tourist town. If you tax something, you get less of it."

A second reading of the tourist tax bill was passed earlier this month in the House of Commons, and forms part of the Labour government's devolution plans.

The government said the legislation would give local authorities the power to raise money from overnight stays and reinvest it in local services and infrastructure.

In Fylde, councillor Cheryl Little, one of seven speaking out against the tax at the council meeting, said: "Tourism is a cornerstone of our economy and visitors support jobs and contribute significantly to the progress of our town.

"The last thing our hospitality trade needs is the administration of an additional tax."

Elsewhere, in Greater Manchester, Mayor Bev Craig has welcomed a visitor levy and does not think it would discourage tourists.

She said: "This charge lets us put that investment into the services that we need to keep the city clean, the trams moving and helps us plan for the future."

Craig added that visitors spending hundreds of pounds on hotel stays would be unlikely to be deterred by a relatively small additional charge.

In a separate scheme introduced last year, a number of hotels in Liverpool agreed to impose a £2 overnight charge - arguing such a charge would raise over £6m in two years for the area.

articles.title: Bill Maher says both Trump and Obama have more common sense than critics on either side would admit
articles.summary: Bill Maher and Piers Morgan agree Donald Trump and Barack Obama are less extreme than critics claim, citing Obama's deportations and Trump's NATO stance.
articles.body: Talk show hosts Bill Maher and Piers Morgan agreed that both President Donald Trump and former President Barack Obama have more common sense and are ultimately less extreme than how they are portrayed by their critics. Maher, a lifelong liberal who criticizes both sides of politics, looked at the current administration as well as the Obama years. When asked who the greatest president of his lifetime would be, however, he answered it would definitely be Obama, or "No Drama Obama," as he later referred to him. "The first Black president of the United States. That's a pretty hard thing to achieve. a very important thing to have had happen in this country. It's why I donated a million dollars to his re-election campaign, because I thought it was even more important that the first Black president be re-elected. And he also did an amazing job," Maher said. Morgan praised Obama for having common sense, saying, "My liberal friends don't even know this fact, but I know you've talked about it, but he deported over 3 million people. He was very tough on immigration." Maher in turn recalled that Obama was nicknamed the "Deporter-in-Chief" and had told conservatives during a meeting with Trump that Obama had "droned a lot of Afghan weddings." DAVID MARCUS: BILL MAHER'S NO REPUBLICAN, HE'S JUST A RARE DEMOCRAT WHO THINKS "There was a lot of Afghan weddings that started with, 'Do you take the' 'What?'" Maher said, appearing to joke about weddings being struck by drones. "Kept Guantanamo Bay open, which we always vowed to shut," Morgan replied. "Yes. Also Obamacare, his signature domestic program, was paid for! So I said, you know, when you guys try to present him as some sort of far-left hippie, your racism is showing," Maher said. Then on Trump, he also offered mixed praise. He first balked when asked by Morgan where Trump would rank among the likes of Obama, but acknowledged that, in political terms, Trump had "the greatest comeback ever." He also suggested that Trump's critics hate him so much that they cannot see how he made necessary reforms. "They hate him so much that they also have to hate the ballroom or whatever. And I don't hate the ballroom. So inconsequential. Actually needed!" Maher said. "When you hate him as much as people hate him, then everything he does is fodder for ridicule, and not every idea he had was bad. You know, I mean, America was a town that needed a lot of cleaning up. And he was like a corrupt sheriff." Morgan added, "I mean, he was right about NATO not pulling their weight on funding. He was right about shutting the southern border. He's been right about a lot of stuff." "Yes! Yes," Maher agreed. BILL MAHER CREDITS TRUMP’S ‘KICK-A--’ CRIME APPROACH AS VIOLENT OFFENSES FALL ACROSS AMERICA Maher specifically highlighted Trump's actions against far-left activism on campuses. "Well, he was also right about colleges have become out of control. Colleges are way too indoctrinated as opposed to just teaching and stuff," Maher said. "The problem is most of the ways he went about doing it went too far or went off the tracks or was or were helmed by idiots, because that's who he has in the administration. Not competent people, people who were loyal because that's the only thing he cares about. So you have morons doing – trying to carry out ideas that in some cases were good ideas." GOP strategist Mary Marslender wrote to Fox News, saying that the two hosts accurately pointed out that Trump’s critics are so blinded by their dislike of him that they refuse to acknowledge his accomplishments. "Morgan and Maher prove the point that Trump Derangement Syndrome is real," she said, agreeing with the talk show hosts. "Many on the left are unable to see past their hatred of Donald Trump to realize the policies that he’s promoting actually make their lives and all Americans' lives better." She concluded, "Obama did deport millions as president, but when the mainstream media idolize you, they conveniently ignore the facts. Enforcing border policy and keeping a nation secure should be a bipartisan issue." Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and to representatives of Obama for comment. articles.title: Princess of Wales visits Hugo Burge Foundation near Duns
articles.summary: The Hugo Burge Foundation gives hundreds of thousands of pounds in grants to art and craft projects.
articles.body:
The Princess of Wales has been in the Scottish Borders to see the work of an arts organisation that is helping to support projects across the UK.

The Hugo Burge Foundation (HBF) which has three bases in the region - one of them on the Marchmont Estate near Duns - carries the name of the internet entrepreneur and philanthropist who died in 2023 aged 51.

The princess - who is known as the Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland - got a glimpse of the work being carried out by the group.

Gardens open to public for first time in decades

Artist Andy Goldsworthy on gathering gravestones: This is my best work yet

She was welcomed by Lucy Brown, HBF chief executive, and learned more about its work supporting creativity and craftsmanship.

She also spent time talking to head gardener Toby Loveday and creative director James Fox during her time in the Borders.

The HBF offers grants, prizes, residencies and studio spaces to artists and craftspeople and provides funding to arts organisations and community groups.

It also funds major public art projects with the goal of "permanently enriching Britain's cultural landscape".

Established in 2022, last year it distributed more than £400,000 of grant funding to individuals, communities, organisations and projects.

Across its three locations, it offers a range of workspaces including a community pottery studio, a state-of-the-art silversmithing workshop, a printmaking studio, and a traditional chairmaking workshop.

It also safeguards a nationally important collection of modern British art.

On its main campus it offers funded residencies throughout the year and cares for a walled garden.

In 2026, it opened Rhymer's Works, a new creative hub in the town of Earlston that offers subsidised studios and community spaces.

articles.title: The alcohol question that should never be asked at holiday parties, experts say

articles.body: With holiday gathering season already here, a recent survey reveals a growing social consensus: More than half of Americans agree that asking someone at a party why they aren't drinking alcohol is a major etiquette faux pas. GLP-1 BOOM COULD RESHAPE RESTAURANT BARS AS DINERS CUT BACK ON ALCOHOL "The proper etiquette worldwide is to not ask anyone. … Don't assume that someone is a drinker." When faced with the uncomfortable question, Burdette suggested that people keep their response simple, graceful and brief. "I would politely say, ‘I choose not to drink’ and smile, but say it in a soft-spoken manner. And then I would redirect the conversation to something that's happy," Burdette advised. "It is not proper to not take a toast when a toast is being given," Burdette noted, but she emphasized that raising a glass filled with water or ginger ale is fully aligned with high-level international etiquette. Should social blunders occur — whether it's an overly personal question that's asked or an awkward comment that's made — Burdette said she advocates for swift grace rather than debate. articles.title: 'Torture with legal cover': Report exposes Israel's abuse of Palestinian prisoners
articles.summary: Israel has allegedly given torture a legal cover to extract confessions from Palestinian detainees.
articles.body: Israel has allegedly given torture a legal cover to extract confessions from Palestinian detainees.A new report claims the country's security agencies have institutionalised abusive interrogation methods, allowing officials to operate with little fear of prosecution.The Guardian, reporting on the findings of the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI), said the report examined 42 complaints filed by Palestinian detainees against Shin Bet interrogators.More than three-quarters of those examined said they had confessed after being subjected to torture or other unlawful interrogation methods.The report documented several methods allegedly used during interrogations, including prolonged sleep deprivation, physical assaults, painful stress positions, threats and sexual violence.Sleep deprivation emerged as one of the most frequently reported practices, with detainees describing being kept awake for extended periods to break their resistance and force confessions.One of the most striking cases involved a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019. According to the report, he was questioned for more than 552 hours over 27.5 days, averaging around 20 hours of interrogation daily. One session reportedly lasted nearly 48 hours. Despite his allegations of abuse, the state inspector concluded that the interrogation had followed established procedures.The findings also raise questions over a 1999 ruling by Israel's Supreme Court, which barred the Shin Bet from using physical pressure as a routine interrogation method. The ruling prohibited practices such as violent shaking and painful restraint positions, while also restricting the deliberate use of sleep deprivation during questioning.However, the court left room for interrogators to invoke a 'necessity defence' in exceptional circumstances, particularly when they claimed that coercive measures were needed to prevent an imminent threat to human life. PCATI alleges that this narrow exception has since been used to justify abusive interrogation practices.The report also questioned the effectiveness of Israel's mechanism for investigating allegations against Shin Bet interrogators. PCATI said more than 1,680 complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024, but none resulted in an indictment. In five cases, the oversight body recommended criminal investigations, but these were eventually closed without prosecutions.The findings come amid concerns over Israel's death penalty legislation, passed by the Knesset in March 2026, which allows capital punishment for Palestinians convicted of certain deadly terrorism-related offences. PCATI warned that convictions based on confessions allegedly extracted through torture could have irreversible consequences.Israel's justice ministry rejected the allegations, saying complaints against Shin Bet interrogators are examined and have led to investigations, disciplinary action and changes to internal procedures, The Times of Israel reported.The controversy has renewed scrutiny of Israel's compliance with international conventions prohibiting torture and its obligations to ensure that confessions obtained through coercion are not used as evidence. PCATI has called for greater accountability and an end to interrogation practices that violate detainees' rights.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Centre may amend defeated women's reservation Bill ahead of special Parliament sitting: Report
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet is scheduled to discuss the delimitation-linked women's reservation Bill at a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet is scheduled to discuss the delimitation-linked women's reservation Bill at a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday, ahead of the special sitting of Parliament beginning November 30, sources said.The meeting has been convened at 1 pm at Sewa Teerth, with all ministers asked to ensure their presence, the sources said on Thursday.The government may consider amendments to the earlier version of the Bill, which seeks to provide 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, they added.The Centre has proposed reconvening the Lok Sabha on November 30 and the Rajya Sabha on December 2 to transact essential government business. Both Houses may conclude their sittings on December 3, depending on the requirements of the business, parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said.The proposed sitting will be an extension of the Monsoon Session, which was adjourned sine die on August 13 but has not been prorogued.This allows the Houses to be reconvened at short notice. Prime Minister Modi had told ministers at Wednesday's Cabinet meeting to remain available in the coming days and postpone visits outside Delhi.Bill seeks to expand Lok Sabha strength to 850The government is seeking to push through the Constitution amendment Bill, which was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April after failing to secure the required two-thirds majority.The legislation proposes increasing the strength of the Lok Sabha from its current 543 seats to a maximum of 850 through delimitation. The exercise is linked to the implementation of 33 per cent reservation for women in Parliament and state legislatures ahead of the 2029 general elections.The Bill requires the support of two-thirds of the members present and voting in the Lok Sabha. With three vacancies, the House currently has 540 members, and the government would need at least 361 votes if all members are present and voting.The ruling National Democratic Alliance has around 320 MPs and would need support from outside its ranks to secure the required numbers.The House would also have to be in order when the Bill is put to vote, as it cannot be passed amid disruptions.The political arithmetic has changed since the Bill's defeat in April, with 26 MPs moving out of the opposition camp.Twenty rebel Trinamool Congress MPs broke away and merged with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), pledging support to the NDA, while six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs joined the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena.The government would still require additional support. The DMK, with 22 Lok Sabha MPs, and the NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar), with eight, could therefore play a significant role in the numbers required for the Bill's passage.Congress accuses Centre of seeking to revive defeated BillThe proposed sitting has drawn criticism from the Congress, which has alleged that the government intends to bring back the delimitation legislation.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh accused the Centre of using the special sitting to secure the numbers needed to pass the Constitution amendment Bill. In a post on X on Thursday, he said:“On the evening of Ambedkar Jayanti on April 14, 2026, the Modi Govt had made the Delimitation Bills public that met their well-deserved fate on the night of April 17, 2026. Now on Constitution Day, after 105 days of Operation Lotus, the Modi Govt announces a special session, hoping that it will get its super-tainted two-thirds majority to pass a Constitution amendment bill. Can there be a great insult to and assault on the Constitution? The fight is on.”Ramesh's remarks came after Rijiju announced the proposed dates for reconvening both Houses. The minister said the government had requested the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Rajya Sabha Chairman to resume proceedings to transact essential government business.The Congress Parliamentary Strategy Group is also scheduled to meet in Delhi on Friday at 4.30 pm to discuss its approach to the parliamentary sitting.The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16, alongside the Delimitation Bill and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill. It failed to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority on April 17 and was not passed.The NDA has maintained that delimitation is necessary to reflect new census data and facilitate women's reservation.The opposition INDIA bloc, led by the Congress, has instead demanded that the 33 per cent quota be implemented in the existing 543-member Lok Sabha, opposing its linkage to delimitation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Guinea-Bissau military leaders delay presidential election until 2028
articles.summary: Military leaders say presidential and legislative poll scheduled for December 6 will now take place in November 2028.
articles.body:
Guinea-Bissau’s military leaders have delayed next month’s presidential and legislative election by two years, pushing back a vote that was meant to return the country to civilian rule.

A decree issued ⁠⁠on Thursday by the transitional president, Major-General Horta Inta-a , said the elections initially scheduled for December 6 would instead take place in November 2028.

The decree said there was “an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions” necessary to hold the vote.

The army seized power in the West African country last November , disrupting a presidential vote and overthrowing the incumbent, Umaro Sissoco Embalo, who was seeking a new ⁠⁠term.

The coup inaugurated former army chief of staff Inta-a as head of the military government, tasked with overseeing a one-year transition period.

The transitional charter published in early December barred Inta-a from running for election.

In August , voters approved a constitutional change ⁠⁠that gives the president more powers.

Last month, Prime Minister Ilidio ⁠⁠Vieira Te said the necessary conditions ⁠⁠were not in place for elections in December, though he did not provide a new timeline.

The regional bloc, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), ⁠⁠had called for a short, structured and transparent transition back to civilian rule.

Guinea-Bissau, one of the world’s poorest countries, has been dogged by coups and attempted coups since its independence from Portugal more than 50 years ago.

The country of 2.2 million people is known as a hub for drug trafficking between Latin America and Europe – a trend that experts say has fuelled its political crises.

West Africa has seen a wave of coups since 2020.

articles.title: Three charts that show how UK net migration surged and then fell
articles.body:
Patterns of people moving to and leaving the UK have changed significantly over the past few decades, with the latest data showing that net migration has hit its lowest non-pandemic level since 1997.

Thursday's Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show 77,000 more people entered from other countries - and stayed for at least 12 months - than left to move abroad in the year leading up to June.

This is a huge fall since nearly a million people were added to the UK's population only three years ago.

You have to go back more than half a century to appreciate just how unusual the last few years have been.

The net migration figure is the balance of two trends - people coming into the country, immigration, and emigration, which is people leaving.

As you can see from this chart, more people were emigrating from the UK for much of the 1960s and 1970s than were coming to stay.

More migrants arriving than leaving became the norm around the same time as the relaxation of European Union (EU) immigration rules in 1993, with net migration rising further after several eastern European countries joined as member nations in the mid-2000s.

Emigration has been drifting up gradually over the past few years, as shown in the grey line in the graph below.

But the real story of the 2020s has been the sharp rise and fall in immigration, the trend of which almost exactly follows that of net migration.

These trends have largely been shaped by a significant increase in non-EU citizens arriving on study or work visas, often bringing families with them, since the government introduced a new immigration system in 2021 after Brexit.

There was also a spike in people seeking humanitarian protection from two specific events for which the government introduced new visa routes:

People leaving Hong Kong in 2021 following the Chinese government's imposition of a strict security law in response to protest and unrest

Ukrainians fleeing Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022

Following this post-Brexit surge, referred to by critics as the "Boriswave", subsequent Conservative and Labour governments increased restrictions on legal migration.

These included raising salary requirements, limiting which workers and students could bring family members and restricting the types of jobs eligible for work visas.

You can see the rise in each of these reasons for coming to the UK in the chart below, as well as the post-restrictions fall, in this chart:

articles.title: A Florida widow won nearly $34.7 million in damages after suing a tobacco company over her husband's death; on November 25, an appeals court reversed the fraud findings and ordered a new damages trial
articles.summary: A Florida appeals court overturned key parts of a widow's lawsuit against tobacco giant R.J.
articles.body: A Florida appeals court overturned key parts of a widow's lawsuit against tobacco giant R.J. Reynolds, setting aside a fraud verdict and ordering a new trial to decide damages after a jury awarded her nearly $34.7 million over her husband's death. The First District Court of Appeal ruled on 25 November 2026 that the widow did not show enough proof that her husband relied on the tobacco company's statements about smoking's health effects or addictiveness, telling the trial judge to rule for Reynolds on the fraud claims and hold a new trial on compensatory and punitive damages. The case was brought by Frances Bessent-Dixon, both on her own and as personal representative for her late husband, Tyrone M. Dixon, after the first jury awarded $8,975,000 in compensatory damages and another $25,748,176 in punitive damages for a total of $34,723,176.The jury's $34.7 million awardThe award came after a trial in Alachua County, Florida, where the jury sided with Bessent-Dixon, finding R.J. Reynolds 60 per cent responsible and Dixon 40 per cent responsible with a verdict that included $8.975 million in compensatory damages and $25,748,176 in punitive damages, according to Courtroom View Network, which covered the trial. Courtroom View Network also reported that Tyrone Dixon died of throat cancer after smoking most of his life, with his family arguing R.J. Reynolds hid the dangers of smoking and its ads shaped his choices, while company lawyers argued Dixon knew the risks but did not try to quit. The case has gone through several trials and appeals, including a 2018 jury trial that ended in a mistrial during the punitive damages phase, according to Courtroom View Network. A later verdict was also challenged, and in January 2021, Florida's First District Court of Appeal overturned that judgment and ordered a new trial because the jury was not properly told that the family had to prove Dixon relied on a false statement by Reynolds for the fraud claim, before the case went back to trial in April 2024 and produced the $34.7 million verdict now under appeal.Why the appeals court rejected the fraud claimsIn its 25 November ruling, the First District Court of Appeal looked at whether Dixon relied on statements from R.J. Reynolds or its predecessors about smoking, explaining that under Florida law, a claim of fraudulent concealment or conspiracy to hide information in this kind of tobacco suit requires proof that the smoker relied on a misleading statement and was harmed by it. The judges agreed Dixon saw plenty of Reynolds ads, noting witnesses said he lived in places where Kool and Newport cigarette promotions were common, collected branded clothes, clipped coupons, joined two promotions, and switched to Newport cigarettes after seeing ads in corner shops. The widow's expert witness, epidemiologist Dr. Michael Cummings, testified about the company's targeted ads and said Dixon's smoking habits matched the advertising, which the trial court relied on along with Dixon's ongoing smoking and his remarks to his wife that there was "nothing wrong with smoking". Yet the appeals court said seeing ads did not, by itself, prove Dixon believed a specific statement about smoking and acted on it, stating the proof needed to link a specific company statement to his beliefs and choices.The court noted every fact witness testified that Dixon never tied his smoking choices or beliefs to tobacco company statements or ads, one witness remembered he mocked cigarette ads, and proof also showed he started smoking because he thought it was "cool" and had seen his parents smoke. His choice of menthol cigarettes was tied to their taste and his belief that menthol went easier on his throat, and even though he told his wife there was "nothing wrong with smoking", the court said the proof did not show when he said it, what prompted it, or how he formed that belief. The judges also looked at Dr. Cummings' testimony that tobacco companies helped spread doubt about smoking's health risks, saying that did not prove Dixon received, believed, and acted on a statement made by Reynolds. The ruling said the jury would have had to make several assumptions to hold the company responsible for Dixon's beliefs and continued smoking, and finding the proof did not back those conclusions, ruled the fraud claims should not have gone to the jury.Dispute over race-targeted advertising evidenceR.J. Reynolds also challenged the use of proof and arguments about its ads aimed at specific racial groups, arguing the trial court wrongly let the jury see this material. The appeals court did not decide if the proof should eventually be allowed, finding instead that the trial judge did not do the legal review needed to weigh the company's First Amendment rights on commercial speech and sending that issue back to the lower court for the required review without saying the ad evidence must be kept out.Why a new damages trial was orderedThe appeals court also ruled that dropping the fraud claims meant the damages award could not stand because the jury weighed the fraud claims alongside the other claims when deciding fault and payout amounts. Even though the strict liability and negligence claims rested on different legal grounds, the judges said the fraud claims were part of the same case put before the jury, creating a fair chance the proof and arguments on fraud shaped the jury's damages decisions. The court said the compensatory and punitive awards could not be split from the claims wrongly given to the jury, ordering a new trial to decide both whether to award damages and, if so, how much. The ruling tells the lower court to enter judgment for R.J. Reynolds on the claims of fraudulent concealment and conspiracy to commit fraudulent concealment, review the disputed race-targeted ad proof under the right First Amendment standard, and hold a new trial on compensatory and punitive damages. The decision was unanimous, with judges Kelsey, M.K. Thomas, and Long concurring, reversing the amended final judgment without throwing out the separate strict liability and negligence claims that still matter in the new damages trial. The case will go back to the Alachua County Circuit Court, where the trial judge must follow the directions from the First District Court of Appeal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: Nine people are injured, three critically, after an explosion at Bangchak Corporation's oil refinery in Bangkok, Thailand, as residents get phone alerts.
articles.body: At least nine people have been injured in an oil refinery explosion in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday, with three in critical condition. The explosion occurred at a Bangchak Corporation-owned facility, the company confirmed in a statement posted to Facebook. The company also claimed it was able to control and extinguish a large blaze caused by the explosion within 30 minutes of the blast. EMERGENCY CREWS RESPONDING TO MASSIVE EXPLOSION AT NEW ORLEANS-AREA OIL REFINERY: SHERIFF Additionally, it claimed monitoring showed no reduction in normal air quality. "Since the incident occurred, the company has continuously monitored air quality in real time using automatic ambient air quality monitoring (AQM) stations, which the company has installed in the Phra Khanong, Bang Na, and Bang Nam Phueng areas to measure air quality around the refinery resulting from operations," the company wrote. TWO INJURED AFTER EXPLOSION RIPS THROUGH CHEMICAL PLANT, SPARKING HAZMAT RESPONSE, SHELTER-IN-PLACE ORDER "It was found that the air quality in the surrounding area of the refinery is within normal standards. Furthermore, at 5: 30 PM (17: 30 hrs.), the Pollution Control Department measured the air quality within a 3–4 km radius around the refinery—the same radial area—and confirmed that the measurement results are within normal standards," the statement added. The company said it has also paused all production operations at the facility. articles.title: Durham councillors reject Murton solar farm plan
articles.summary: Grupotec Solar UK 9 Limited had wanted to install panels and battery storage facilities in Murton.
articles.body:
Plans for a major solar farm on the outskirts of a village have been refused.

Grupotec Solar UK 9 Limited wanted to install panels and battery storage facilities on a 120 hectare site on South Sharpley Farm in Murton, County Durham.

Farmer and landowner Jo Hare argued the solar farm would "protect the future" of his family's farm, but campaigners said it would harm the landscape.

Despite being recommended for approval, Durham County Council's (DCC) planning committee voted to reject the plans. Sunderland City Council is yet to make a decision on part of the scheme within its boundary.

Grupotec Solar UK 9 Limited said the farm would help "decarbonise" the electricity network and aid the UK in achieving its net zero targets.

But campaigners from the East Durham Action Group said the plans would be "really devastating".

Dr Brian Brown told the committee the scheme would "engulf" the nearby village, which would be "grossly unfair" to residents.

He said the plan should not be considered on its own but rather councillors should take into account ongoing applications for similar schemes in the area.

The authority received 45 objections, including from Seaham Town Council and Murton Parish Council, and seven letters of support.

Urging committee members to approve the scheme, Hare said the solar farm on his land would provide needed additional income.

"Farmers are facing a very difficult time at the moment," he said, citing rising costs, and unpredictable weather.

The solar scheme would allow him to increase the size of his sheep flock and "potentially buy more land to farm, just securing the future of the farm", he added.

The solar farm was "expected to generate enough clean renewable electricity to offset the annual electricity usage of more than 13,000 homes", the council report said.

Construction would take a year and it would occupy the site for 40 years, with the land to be reinstated at the end over a 12 month period, the report said.

Councillors rejected the scheme, which Scott Woodhouse, Reform's DCC planning and highway committee chairman, said was a "big win" for residents.

But, he warned, the decision could be appealed and he believed it would have a "big chance of winning".

It was "only the start of the journey", Brown said.

articles.title: An Ohio woman fired her lawyers, secured a $250,000 car-accident settlement herself and faced legal-fee claims; November 25 judges ruled her firm must prove the reasonable value of its work, not a contract percentage
articles.summary: An Ohio woman let her lawyers go and worked out a $250,000 car crash settlement on her own, winning part of an appeal over the legal fees her old law firm
articles.body: An Ohio woman let her lawyers go and worked out a $250,000 car crash settlement on her own, winning part of an appeal over the legal fees her old law firm claimed. On 25 November 2026, the Eighth District Court of Appeals ruled that Rumizen Weisman Co., Ltd. cannot figure out its fee just by using the percentage in its original contingency contract, requiring the firm instead to show the fair value of the legal work it did before she let it go. The court backed the firm's right to ask for payment through a legal charging lien and a breach-of-contract claim, yet threw out the dollar amount set by the lower court and sent the fee fight back for a new look under a legal rule called quantum meruit. The case involves Amber Kopanski, who got $250,000 from her insurer, Progressive Direct Insurance Company, after ending her work with the firm, whereas the earlier court order gave the firm $74,035.98 covering $63,333.33 in legal fees and $10,702.65 in costs.How the legal dispute beganAccording to the court ruling, Kopanski hired Rumizen Weisman on 14 April 2022 to handle her injuries and losses from a car crash under a contingency-fee contract, meaning the firm would get a share of any money won. The firm filed a lawsuit for her on 1 June 2022 in the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas against the driver who caused the crash and Progressive, which was part of an underinsured motorist claim, working for Kopanski for about two years while paying case costs up front and working to get her money.A private mediation happened on 11 April 2024, where Progressive offered $190,000 according to a sworn statement from the firm's lawyer, Mitchell A. Weisman, while the mediator and the other side's lawyer also said the insurer would have paid $250,000 if Kopanski had taken that deal. Kopanski turned down the offer and mediation ended with no deal, leading her to drop her lawsuit on her own on 30 April 2024, officially let Rumizen Weisman go as her lawyers on 17 May, and make a deal straight with Progressive in late June 2024 for a $250,000 cheque.Former firm demanded paymentThe settlement did not end the fight between Kopanski and her old lawyers, so on 9 July 2024, Rumizen Weisman sued her in a separate case claiming she owed money for the legal work and costs it covered while representing her. Its lawsuit raised claims for breach of contract, unjust enrichment, and conversion and asked for a charging lien on the settlement funds, a legal claim that can let a lawyer get unpaid fees out of money won through the lawyer's work. The firm said its contract let it collect costs and legal fees if Kopanski ended things, basing the fee on the last settlement offer or the value of the work done before dismissal, whichever was higher, and told Kopanski in a letter sent by email and FedEx on 2 July 2024 that it planned to seek a charging lien for $10,702.65 in costs plus legal fees figured as one-third of the $190,000 offer made at mediation. Kopanski pushed back against the claim in a 19 May 2024 email to Weisman, saying there was no formal written offer and arguing that the failed mediation did not force her to pay a fee based on an offer she did not take. She also filed a counterclaim for legal malpractice, which the trial court threw out in November 2024.Why the lower court awarded $74,035Rumizen Weisman asked the trial court for summary judgment, arguing the signed contract and its past work gave it a clear right to payment, and turned in sworn statements from its lawyers, the fee contract, emails and letters with Kopanski, a report on mediation, and a list of case costs it paid. One sworn statement said the firm's work and legal skill helped bring about the $190,000 mediation offer, another lawyer representing the driver at fault backed up that Progressive made that offer and later settled directly with Kopanski for $250,000, and an accountant's sworn statement confirmed the firm paid $10,702.65 in case costs. Kopanski agreed she signed the contingency contract, the firm represented her for two years, and it gave legal help and paid costs, as well as agreeing she let the firm go and later settled directly with Progressive. The trial court granted summary judgment to Rumizen Weisman, giving it $63,333.33 in legal fees (one-third of the $190,000 mediation offer) plus $10,702.65 in costs for a total of $74,035.98, which Kopanski appealed by arguing the firm did not show its fees were fair or matched the worth of the work it finished.Appeals court says contract percentage cannot decide the feeIn its 25 November ruling, the Eighth District Court of Appeals agreed with Kopanski on how to figure legal fees, saying Ohio law does not let a fired contingency lawyer simply take the percentage written in the contract, but instead lets the lawyer ask for the fair worth of the work done before the relationship ended. That rule is called quantum meruit, which lets a person get paid a fair amount for work done for someone else, and the court pointed to past Ohio Supreme Court rulings including Cuyahoga County Bar Association v. Levey and Reid, Johnson, Downes, Andrachik & Webster v. Lansberry holding that a fired lawyer's pay must match the fair value of completed work rather than just the original contingency percentage. The judges said a court looking at the fee should weigh several things, including hours worked before dismissal, money sought, skill needed, results reached, and the contract between lawyer and client, ruling that the lower court skipped that review by using the one-third fee math without finding the real value of the firm's work. The judges also cited a 2024 Ohio appeals ruling about another client who let a firm go and later settled on her own, where that court also ruled the firm had to show proof of the fair value of its work before getting fees.What happens nextThe appeals court did not rule that Rumizen Weisman gets zero pay, keeping the firm's right to seek a charging lien and sue for breach of contract after finding Kopanski signed the contract, got legal work, and did not pay the costs and fees claimed, while throwing out the $74,035.98 award because the fee used the contract percentage instead of the fair value of the work. The case now goes back to the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas only to decide how much the firm can recover under quantum meruit. Judge Eileen A. Gallagher wrote the ruling, with Presiding Judge Eileen T. Gallagher and Judge Sean C. Gallagher joining, as the appeals court kept part of the lower court's ruling, threw out the fee award, and ordered more steps. The new review will decide what the firm gets paid for work done before Kopanski let it go, while the $250,000 settlement itself stays the amount she got from Progressive.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kashmir clerics split over Vande Mataram
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: A religious dispute over Vande Mataram at official functions in Kashmir escalated Thursday, with Sunni scholar Maulana Abdul Rashid Dawoodi
articles.body: SRINAGAR: A religious dispute over Vande Mataram at official functions in Kashmir escalated Thursday, with Sunni scholar Maulana Abdul Rashid Dawoodi challenging clerics to issue a fatwa on standing during its rendition and J&K’s grand mufti Nasir-ul-Islam declaring participation impermissible under Islamic law.Dawoodi urged scholars to settle whether standing for the national song as protocol amounted to polytheism or disbelief. “If any authentic organisation says that standing for Vande Mataram amounts to polytheism or disbelief, let it come forward with a fatwa,” he said.Dawoodi faced criticism after attending a J&K Waqf Board function in Srinagar on Monday, where all six stanzas of the song were played. He said standing as a matter of protocol should not automatically be equated with worship and accused critics of targeting him. “You cannot make statements recklessly,” he said, urging scholars to issue a fatwa on the specific question.The song was played under a Union home ministry protocol directive issued earlier this year mandating its full rendition at official functions, state events and legislature sessions.But grand mufti Nasir-ul-Islam, who heads the Muslim Personal Law Board, said attending a programme where Vande Mataram was sung or participating in its rendition was impermissible under Islamic law, citing sharia’s prohibition on worshipping created beings or bowing before them.Several clerics who attended Monday’s Waqf Day event, attended by Union minority affairs minister Kiren Rijiju, waqf board chairperson Darakhshan Andrabi and Lok Sabha MP Mian Altaf Ahmad, expressed regret on Wednesday and said they had prayed for repentance.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Ukrainian intelligence says North Korea paused missile deliveries to Russia amid friction over South Korea
articles.summary: North Korea paused ballistic missile and artillery shipments to Russia after friction over Moscow's outreach to South Korea, Ukrainian intelligence said.
articles.body: North Korea has temporarily halted shipments of ballistic missiles and artillery shells to Russia following diplomatic friction between the two allies over Moscow's outreach to South Korea, Ukrainian military intelligence said Thursday. According to Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency, North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui announced the freeze on KN-23 ballistic missile and artillery deliveries last month after Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko suggested Moscow would help de-escalate tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang, Reuters reported. Choe demanded that Russia clarify its policy toward South Korea, GUR said, though Reuters noted it could not independently verify the report or confirm public remarks from either official. PUTIN'S WAR DEATH TOLL REPORTEDLY TOPS 700,000 AS RUSSIA SCRAMBLES FOR RECRUITS The reported pause also suspends Russian military flights over North Korea and stalls a Kremlin request to expand North Korea's troop deployment in Russia from roughly 8,500 to 50,000, according to the outlet. Rudenko, who oversees Asian relations, said last month that Seoul had signaled interest in normalizing ties and resuming direct flights with Moscow once the Ukraine war ends. Despite the reported freeze, North Korean troops remain active in Russia, with 11th Corps units serving in the Kursk region and a missile unit operating in Voronezh since mid-summer, GUR said. Russian President Vladimir Putin also hosted top Kim Jong Un aide Jo Yong Won at the Kremlin last week, where both men reportedly praised bilateral cooperation. Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on social media Thursday that Moscow is "completing preparations for a new massive strike" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, logistics and critical services. TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE Crews are already working to restore power in six regions after overnight Russian missile and drone strikes damaged an apartment building, a hospital and businesses, according to Zelenskyy, who also renewed appeals for U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors. articles.title: Net migration to UK tumbles by 92% from its peak, but Indians still most common nationality to immigrate to Britain
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from London: Figures from the UK’s Office of National Statistics, released Thursday, show that long-term international net migration to
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from London: Figures from the UK’s Office of National Statistics, released Thursday, show that long-term international net migration to the country stood at just 77,000 in the year ending June 2026, the lowest for 30 years, excluding the pandemic.The 77,000 figure is the first time the UK has seen net migration (difference between long-term immigration and emigration) in the tens of thousands since former UK PM David Cameron’s pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level. This is a fall of 92% compared to the year ending March 2023, when net migration peaked at 944,000.Approximately 738,000 people moved to the UK and 661,000 left in the year to June 2026. The fall has been driven by non-EU+ immigration falling by more than 100,000 due to visa reforms introduced by the last Conservative govt and Labour.During the year ending June 2026, non-EU+ nationals accounted for 75% of total immigration at 550,000; 47% came for study-related reasons, 25% for work-related reasons, and 13% were for asylum-related reasons. There were just 79,000 EU+ nationals immigrating in the year ending June 2026.The number of people immigrating for asylum-related reasons decreased to 73,000 in the year ending June 2026, down from 93,000 the previous year.Indian remains the most common nationality to immigrate to the UK, totalling 123,000 in the year ending June 2026, with study-related reasons being the top reason (77,000 visas) followed by work (40,000 visas).Yet the number of Indians immigrating has fallen by more than 50% compared to YE June 2023, when 307,000 Indians immigrated to the UK, of which 159,000 came on study visas, and 136,000 came on work visas.Indians are also now the largest group to emigrate from the UK in the year ending June 2026, with 85,000 leaving, of whom 55,000 had come on study visas and 28,000 on work visas.You use AI every day. articles.title: Attack on Saudi’s Jazan refinery kills one person, disrupts operations
articles.summary: The attack killed a Nepali national, injured several people and sparked a fire, Saudi Energy Ministry says.
articles.body:
An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy.

Thursday’s attack on the facility on the kingdom’s Red Sea coast caused a fire and temporarily halted some operations, the ministry said.

The statement did not identify who carried out the strike, but earlier the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said that the Iranian-backed group had ⁠⁠attacked the refinery. It came after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency had issued an alert about potential danger in Jazan province.

The strike was the Houthis ‘ latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides.

The Saudi Ministry of Energy said the worker who died was Nepali, while the injured were of various nationalities.

The injured received medical care, while emergency personnel and specialised technical teams arrived at the site to assess the damage and verify the safety of the facilities following the attack, the ministry added.

The refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia , near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

The Saudi-led coalition, which is backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight with the Houthis, condemned the strike and threatened a counterattack.

“Targeting civilians and ⁠⁠civilian infrastructure would ⁠⁠be ⁠⁠met with a firm military ‌‌response,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki posted on X.

Later on Thursday, the coalition claimed its forces had destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s Hodeidah governorate used by the armed group to stage the attack on the Jazan refinery, according to al-Maliki. There was no immediate statement from the Houthis regarding the strike.

On the ground in Yemen, meanwhile, Saudi-backed government forces claimed they had carried out 767 strikes on Houthi positions on Thursday.

In a post on X, the forces’ spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the strikes had “neutralised” 117 Houthi fighters and destroyed 87 vehicles and combat assets.

Al-Nuzaili added that government forces continued to confront Houthi formations on the front lines in northern and western Marib governorate, as well as in the governorates of al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahj, Shabwah and Hajjah.

Earlier on Thursday, a series of air strikes targeted Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, according to media affiliated with the armed group, which is also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.

Elsewhere, Houthi forces targeted Habib al-Sarm and al-Hujalla, as well as al-Aqroud in al-Masrakh district.

The Houthis, who control the most populous areas of Yemen, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since the country’s civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war.

The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football’s AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference.

The fighting has also exacerbated dire humanitarian conditions for Yemeni civilians.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that as of Monday, 2,361 people had been killed and 10,982 injured since fighting in Yemen escalated in August. More than 360,000 people have also been forced to flee their homes in Yemen since the start of August, according to the UN.

articles.title: Supreme Court sets timer for FSSAI, companies to implement warning labels
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has set a timeline to implement the front-of-package labelling for each nutrient of concern on packaged food.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has set a timeline to implement the front-of-package labelling for each nutrient of concern on packaged food.The top court granted four months’ time to food regulator FSSAI to frame rules, and one year’s time to make it compulsory for companies. The labels indicating high sugar, saturated fat and salt will be placed inside red, hexagonal shapes.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran pushed the regulator to fall in line and discharge its duty to protect the interest of consumers, noting that FSSAI showed “reluctance” on labelling followed in many countries to make consumers aware of the harmful contents.Supreme Court said India is facing a major public health crisis, driven in part by the consumption of foods high in saturated fat, sugar and/or salt. “The population’s exposure to harmful substances must be controlled, their consumption must be discouraged, and consumers must be protected from practices detrimental to health used by the food businesses. Preventive measures, that are most effective, must therefore be undertaken in an effort to respect, protect and guarantee the right to health,” the bench said, adding that it cannot remain a “mute spectator” in such a situation.Supreme Court: Every day’s delay allows unlabelled food to be soldSupreme Court bound the regulator to the time frame suggested by it, which was four months to follow the process under the 2006 Act and regulations. It agreed that food business operators be granted a year’s time from the date of notification to implement the labelling regime. The intervening 365 days will be a “voluntary implementation” period.“Every day of delay means that packaged foods continue to be sold without such labels, to the detriment of the rights to health, food and informed choice, respectively... FSSAI should anticipate potential impediments and take active measures to ensure that they are resolved or adequately addressed,” the bench said.“The right to health has expanded from being limited to healthcare to addressing the broader determinants of health and conditions congenial to good health; the right to food now requires access to food which is sufficient in terms of both quantity and quality; and the right to informed choice has expanded its focus towards confronting the broader informational and social order that people live in,” Supreme Court said.It rejected FSSAI’s plea that there be only one hexagon within which levels of ‘high sugar’, ‘high saturated fat’ and ‘high salt’ would be placed, directing there be a separate hexagon for each nutrient of concern. “The font size... must be such that it remains clear, prominent and readily legible alongside pictograms,” Supreme Court added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Netflix’s first original Pakistani series has run into a diplomatic and regulatory hurdle in India even before its global premiere. The ministry of information and broadcasting on Thursday asked the streaming giant to ensure that no content originating in Pakistan is made available to Indian subscribers, following complaints over the possible release of its star-studded romantic drama, Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo.Scheduled for release on December 4, the series features Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Sanam Saeed and Hania Aamir, actors familiar to Indian audiences. Netflix has not clarified whether India is among the markets where the series will be streamed.Government advisory on Pak content issued during Operation SindoorThe ministry’s intervention comes 18 months after government, amid Operation Sindoor, issued an advisory on May 8, 2025, asking digital platforms to discontinue Pakistani-origin films, series, songs, podcasts and other content on national security grounds.Officials said Netflix had informed the ministry in June 2025 that no Pakistani-origin film or series was available to its Indian subscribers. The ministry has now asked it to honour that commitment.When TOI reached out to Netflix, the platform said it had no comment.The controversy escalated after All Indian Cine Workers Association and Federation of Western India Cine Employees approached PM Narendra Modi. All Indian Cine Workers Association has also sought a permanent legal framework prohibiting Pakistani entertainment content in India, while Federation of Western India Cine Employees, an umbrella body of 32 associations representing five lakh workers, threatened to “ensure the shoot of all Netflix projects comes to a halt” if the series is released.Pakistan’s planning and development minister, Ahsan Iqbal, accused India of weaponising art and culture.Directed and produced by Momina Duraid, the series is based on Farhat Ishtiaq’s bestselling 2013 Urdu novel.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A US Air Force pilot bought a wrecked Boeing Stearman on eBay as a restoration project, but its serial number revealed it had trained the Tuskegee Airmen during World War II
articles.summary: A damaged aircraft bought online as a restoration project turned out to have a history its new owners had not expected.
articles.body: A damaged aircraft bought online as a restoration project turned out to have a history its new owners had not expected. US Air Force Captain Matt Quy and his wife, Tina, purchased a wrecked Boeing Stearman biplane on eBay in 2005, hoping to rebuild it and eventually take it flying. As they worked through the extensive repairs, a search into the aircraft's military records revealed that it had once been used to train the Tuskegee Airmen, the pioneering group of Black military pilots who served during World War II. The discovery changed the couple's plans, instead of treating the aircraft as a personal flying project, they began restoring it as a tribute to the men who had trained in it.Matt Quy’s eBay purchase turned out to be a WWII training aircraftMatt Quy had wanted to own a Stearman biplane since childhood. Growing up in Minnesota near a grass airstrip, he regularly watched a neighbour fly the aircraft, an experience that stayed with him long after he began pursuing a career in aviation. Years later, after becoming a pilot, he and his wife Tina decided to look for a biplane of their own.Buying an aircraft in flying condition was beyond their budget. As reported by Associated Press, their search eventually led them to a damaged Boeing PT-13 Stearman listed on eBay. The aircraft had been wrecked in an accident, leaving much of its structure in need of repair. The couple bought it in 2005, knowing that bringing it back into the air would require considerable time, money and mechanical work.At that stage, they were primarily interested in restoring vintage aircraft. Its connection to one of the most significant chapters in American military aviation history was still unknown to them.How a serial number revealed the aircraft's Tuskegee Airmen historyThe turning point came when Quy decided to investigate the aircraft's serial number. He contacted the Air Force Historical Research Agency at Maxwell Air Force Base in Alabama to establish where the plane had served. The records brought an unexpected answer: the Stearman had been assigned to the training programme at Moton Field in Alabama, where Black pilots were prepared for military service during the Second World War.The Air Force confirmed that the aircraft was among those used to train the Tuskegee Airmen. It was no longer simply an old biplane that could be brought back to flying condition. Its wartime service gave it a direct connection to the experiences of the men who had helped break racial barriers in American military aviation.Quy and Tina decided to change the purpose of their restoration project. They named the aircraft ‘The Spirit of Tuskegee’, intending to use it to introduce more people to the history of the airmen and their contribution.The three-year restoration brought the biplane back to lifeThe Stearman had been badly damaged after an earlier engine failure led to an emergency landing on a road, where it struck a tree. Its wings had suffered extensive destruction, while parts of the fuselage, engine, landing gear and braking system also needed attention.Quy took on much of the work outside his military duties, spending his spare time rebuilding the aircraft. Reportedly, his wife helped with the project, as did aircraft mechanic Robbie Vajdos, who worked alongside him on the repairs. They also had to locate replacement components, although the fact that many Stearman aircraft had been converted into agricultural planes after the war meant that some parts could still be sourced.The restoration took approximately three years. By February 2008, the aircraft had returned to the skies, giving the couple an opportunity to see the results of their work. The original wartime appearance was also recreated, with a blue body, yellow wings and red markings on the tail.How the aircraft brought former Tuskegee pilots back togetherRather than keeping the restored biplane as a private possession, Matt and Tina began travelling with it to events across the United States. Over the next six and a half years, they used the aircraft to draw attention to the Tuskegee Airmen and their wartime training.Some of the encounters were particularly meaningful because veterans who had trained in Stearman aircraft were able to see the restored machine again. At an aviation gathering in Reno, Nevada, four Tuskegee veterans were reunited with the aircraft, and all four had an opportunity to fly in it.One of them was retired Lieutenant Colonel Bill Holloman, a fighter pilot who had served during the Second World War and the Korean War. His flight with Quy was his first time in a Stearman since his own pilot training roughly six decades earlier.The Smithsonian became the aircraft's next homeThe story eventually reached Paul Gardullo, a curator involved in preparing the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC. The museum had been looking for an aircraft connected to the Tuskegee Airmen, and information about the Quys' restored Stearman reached him through a colleague at the National Air and Space Museum.Gardullo travelled to an air show at Edwards Air Force Base in California to see the aircraft. The Quys were displaying it alongside Tuskegee veterans, and the curator approached them about the possibility of donating it to the new museum.The couple initially had reservations. They had spent years rebuilding the aircraft and understood that handing it over to a museum could mean the end of its flying days. However, they eventually agreed, recognising that the Smithsonian could give the aircraft a permanent place in a much wider account of African American military history.In July 2011, Matt Quy began its final cross-country journey. The couple made stops along the way, including at the Air Force Academy in Colorado, where Tuskegee veterans were waiting to meet the aircraft. The journey also included Moton Field in Alabama, the place where the Stearman had served during the war. The aircraft was subsequently handed over to the Smithsonian.How nearly 1,000 Black pilots trained to serve during World War IIThe restored Boeing Stearman PT-13D is displayed at the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC. Its blue, yellow and red appearance reflects the aircraft's restored wartime design, while its presence in the museum connects visitors with an important part of the history of Black Americans in the armed forces.The Tuskegee Airmen were trained at a time when the US military was segregated. Their training programme operated in and around Tuskegee, Alabama, with Moton Field serving as a primary flight-training site. Nearly 1,000 Black pilots trained there between 1941 and the mid-1940s, overcoming institutional discrimination and restrictions that had long limited their opportunities to serve as military aviators.You use AI every day.
