articles.title: A 65-year-old Australian funeral director lost his job after police revoked a clearance for duties he had stopped performing months earlier; a tribunal has ordered his employer to pay A$48,966 plus superannuation
articles.summary: A 65-year-old funeral director in Australia has been awarded A$48,966 in compensation after his employer dismissed him over a police clearance he no
articles.body: A 65-year-old funeral director in Australia has been awarded A$48,966 in compensation after his employer dismissed him over a police clearance he no longer needed for his daily work. The Fair Work Commission ruled that the company had not established a valid reason to end his employment and ordered it to pay the amount along with superannuation.According to the judgement, the employee had worked at Renshaw’s Funeral Service in Bathurst since July 2016. He was serving as its Lead Funeral Director and Location Manager when Harris McDonald, which operates the funeral home, dismissed him in February 2026.The dispute centred on a clearance issued by New South Wales Police. The approval allowed him to take part in the transfer of bodies on behalf of the state coroner and police. However, this work accounted for only around 5% to 10% of his working time.In November 2025, he had asked the company to remove him and other staff from these duties because of the strain they were causing. The business shifted the work to another funeral home, and he did not carry out any further transfers before losing his job.The issue arose again in January 2026, when police revoked his approval following what they described as an adverse interaction. The employee was on personal leave and unwell at the time. Harris McDonald later told him that he could no longer meet the requirements of his position and ended his employment with effect from February 23.Commission questions the company's decisionHarris McDonald maintained that the police approval was necessary for the employee's role. It also pointed to a clause in his employment contract requiring him to maintain the qualifications and licences needed for his work.The Commission accepted that the clearance was a requirement for the role. However, Deputy President Wright found that its withdrawal did not automatically make the dismissal fair.A key consideration was that the employee had already stopped doing the work covered by the approval, with the company's agreement. The Commission also noted that he was unlikely to be assigned those duties again in the immediate future.The company had not used the dispute-resolution process available under its agreement with the state department to challenge the police decision. Documents later obtained from police also indicated that the employee could apply for approval again.The Deputy President found that police had wrongly described the incident at the employee's home. The decision also noted that there appeared to be no reasonable basis for withdrawing the clearance.The way the company handled the dismissal further counted against it. The process began while the employee was on sick leave. The Commission noted that the company could have waited until he returned, without any harm to its operations.It also found that the employee had not been given sufficient information about the reason for the police decision, making it difficult for him to respond properly.Plans for another mortuary did not justify dismissalHarris McDonald also raised concerns about the employee's plans to establish a mortuary of his own while he was still working for the company.He had lodged a development application for the proposed facility in November 2025. The local council approved it in March 2026, after his dismissal.The Commission accepted that the proposed business could compete with Renshaw’s once it began operating. However, it found no evidence that the employee had approached the company's clients, misused confidential information, worked on the project during company hours or neglected his responsibilities.Simply preparing to start a competing business was not enough to establish a breach of his employment obligations, the Deputy President ruled.Employer ordered to pay A$48,966While assessing compensation, the Commission considered the employee's age, length of service and likely future earnings. It estimated that he could have remained with the company for another 12 months if he had not been dismissed.The initial compensation calculation was higher, but the amount was limited by the legal cap on unfair dismissal payments. The Commission therefore ordered Harris McDonald to pay him A$48,966.06, along with superannuation.The ruling, delivered on November 16, found that the dismissal was harsh, unjust and unreasonable. The company must make the payment by November 30.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Judicial member must on bench to confirm PMLA attachment, says Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In an important insertion into the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, the Supreme Court on Friday said the bench of the adjudicating authority
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In an important insertion into the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, the Supreme Court on Friday said the bench of the adjudicating authority (AA), tasked with deciding the confirmation of ED’s orders for provisional attachment of assets by terming them proceeds of crime, must have a judicial member.Deciding a host of petitions questioning the competence of administrative members forming single-member benches to decide questions of law and conflicting judgements from various HCs, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said that to confirm confiscation of assets termed as ‘proceeds of crime’ under Section 8 of PMLA, the AA is required to analyse legal provisions.“The presence of a judicial member on the bench undertaking the same ensures legal objectivity in the determination recorded by the AA. The lifetime of experience of the administrative and financial members in the AA would undoubtedly render them to be exceptional experts in their fields, but impartial and legally sound adjudication necessitates judicial temperament and training,” the bench said.It added, however, that the judgment would operate prospectively and not provide grounds for the reopening of past decisions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Jeff Bezos reveals he still seeks Barack Obama’s advice, calls Donald Trump the ‘most accessible’ president he has worked with and offers guidance to Nvidia’s board on choosing its next CEO
articles.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has praised US President Donald Trump for being particularly communicative, describing him as the most accessible president he
articles.body: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has praised US President Donald Trump for being particularly communicative, describing him as the most accessible president he has worked with. However, Bezos also revealed that he continues to turn to former President Barack Obama for advice, saying the former president has offered him valuable guidance over the years.Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in Menlo Park, California, on Tuesday, Bezos said he had worked with every US president since Bill Clinton and hoped to maintain that engagement with future administrations.“I've worked with every president since Clinton, and I hope to work with every president going forward as long as they'll have me,” Bezos said. “Trump is particularly communicative. He reaches out a lot.”Jeff Bezos says Donald Trump is more accessible than other presidentsBezos acknowledged that Obama was also highly communicative and said he still seeks his advice.“Clinton and Bush and Obama—Obama was very communicative too, and I still reach out to Obama for advice,” he said. “He's given me some good advice over the years.”However, when it came to the frequency of communication, Bezos said Trump stood apart from his predecessors.“But none of them were half as communicative as Trump is,” he said. “Trump is the most accessible. You can call him, he'll call you.”Bezos clarified that he was referring to the frequency of communication rather than making a qualitative comparison between the presidents.“So he's very unusual in that—not in terms of like qualitatively unusual, just quantitatively,” he said. “Just the amount of outreach is unusual.”He added that he did not know who the next president would be or how much advice that person might want. However, he felt that communication between business leaders and the president was worthwhile.“But I don't think reaching out to the president or vice versa is a bad thing,” Bezos said. “I think it's a good thing, and most presidents do it to one degree or another.”Jeff Bezos says blaming ‘villains’ does not solve real-world problemsThe conversation also covered politics, business and the challenges facing the technology industry. Addressing criticism of wealthy technology leaders, Bezos said identifying a villain could be an effective political strategy but was not a productive way to solve practical problems.“‘Pick a villain’ is a time-tested ancient technique in the political realm. For political campaigns and mobilization, scapegoating is a brilliant political tool; but if you truly want to solve real-world problems, it is the worst technique,” he said.He cited the housing affordability crisis as an example, arguing that increasing the supply of homes was essential to addressing rising costs.“To genuinely lower housing costs, there is only one physically viable path: literally building more houses,” Bezos said.Jeff Bezos discusses his new AI venture PrometheusBezos also spoke about his return to entrepreneurship through Prometheus, an artificial intelligence company he co-founded with Vik Bajaj. The venture is focused on applying AI to physical engineering and manufacturing.He argued that existing large language models are particularly effective at working with text, mathematics and coding but lack the specialised understanding needed to design and manufacture physical products.Bezos said Prometheus is developing specialised models to help engineers work on complex designs, including components such as analogue chips and industrial valves. He described the work as an exciting challenge that made it difficult for him to remain a passive investor.Jeff Bezos offers advice to Nvidia’s board on CEO successionThe Amazon founder also discussed leadership succession at major technology companies. Asked about Nvidia, he advised its board to prioritise internal candidates when selecting a successor.“If I must offer advice to the Nvidia board, it is this: insist on promoting successors from within,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."
authors: Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent

articles.title: Film buff reopens Dumfries cinema that shut eight years ago
articles.summary: Dumfries was left without a large-scale cinema when the Odeon closed its doors in 2018.
articles.body:
There may not be a red carpet - but it is still a big night in the history of cinema in a south of Scotland town.

When the 470-seater former Odeon in Dumfries closed its doors in the summer of 2018 it left it without a large-scale movie theatre.

After more than two years of work, the dream of Elgin-based film fan Tristan Campbell to bring it back to life will come true with a screening of Focker-in-Law starring Robert De Niro, Ariana Grande and Ben Stiller.

It is quite a step up for the whisky distiller - originally from Coleraine - whose only previous experience was a "trial run" with converting his garage into a home cinema.

I scaled up my garage home cinema to a 470-seat movie theatre

Tristan said it had been a "busy few days" as full licensing approval to open the new Regal cinema had only come through on Wednesday evening.

"Myself and some of the team have been working from half past seven in the morning until two o'clock in the morning - tidying up, putting the finishing touches to the place, getting everything ready to go," he said.

"It's just all those little jobs - like even loading the films onto the projector and getting all that ready.

"So it has been frantic, but we're getting there. The end is in sight and it's exciting."

Tristan said he would be "absolutely delighted" to see the cinema full but admitted that even half-full would be great due to the lateness of being able to put tickets on sale.

"There's lots of excitement and lots of nerves as well," he said.

"I'm thinking, oh goodness, you know, what can go wrong? Is there something that I need to be doing? Is there something else we need to check?

"So lots of nerves, but lots of excitement too."

At the time of its closure, the cinema on the town's Shakespeare Street had served Dumfries for almost 90 years, having first opened in the early 1930s.

It went through a number of names - including Regal, ABC, Cannon and Odeon - and was also adapted to include a bingo hall.

Despite an attempt to modernise the facility with a section of more comfortable seating put in, the operators decided to pull the plug in 2018.

Odeon said it had faced "ongoing issues with the building" and went ahead with the closure.

It left Dumfries - a town with a population of about 40,000 - without a cinema other than the much smaller 69-seat council-run Robert Burns Centre.

Residents have had to travel to a small multi-screen site about 15 miles (24km) away in Annan or 30 miles (48km) across the border to Carlisle to see the latest releases.

Tristan said that thanks to strong local support they should now have a facility a little bit closer to home.
